findings.title: Supabase tables reachable with the public anon key because Row Level Security is off or too permissive
findings.description: Supabase-backed apps ship the project URL and anon/publishable key in the client bundle by design. That is only safe when RLS policies are enabled on every table. AI builders often scaffold tables with RLS disabled, or write policies like USING (true), so anyone can call the PostgREST endpoint (/rest/v1/<table>) with the anon key and read or write whole tables without logging in.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: The generated frontend works the same with or without RLS, so nothing looks broken. Novices do not know the anon key needs RLS alongside it, and AI scaffolds have generated schemas without enabling RLS. Lovable's generated projects were assigned CVE-2025-48757 for this pattern.
findings.user_impact: Anyone on the internet can dump every user's PII, payment records, tokens and private messages, and can also change or deface data.
findings.detection_approach: Watch network traffic for *.supabase.co requests and pull the project URL and anon key from the bundle or request headers. From an unauthenticated context, send GET /rest/v1/<table>?select=*&limit=1 for each table name seen in the app's own requests, and for common names (users, profiles, orders, messages) if the user opts in. Flag any rows that come back when they should not, especially rows owned by other test accounts. Use two seeded test accounts to confirm cross-user reads. Keep writes opt-in, since they are destructive.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Matt Palmer's CVE-2025-48757 disclosure, found 2025-03-20 and published 2025-05-29, covers 'insufficient RLS' in Lovable projects. Secondary write-ups report 170 of 1,645 scanned Lovable apps (10.3%) exposed. Wiz (2026-02-02) found Moltbook's missing RLS exposed 1.5M API tokens and 35,000+ emails, with full write access. The Register (2026-02-27) reported a Lovable-showcased app exposing 18,697 user records.
findings.corrections: Attribute 170/1,645 (10.3%) to secondary reporting, not Palmer's post. Add context: Supabase now enables RLS by default on dashboard-created tables and flags RLS-off public tables through the Security Advisor lint 0013_rls_disabled_in_public. The gap remains for tables created via SQL or migrations, which is how AI tools create them. Also note that USING(true) policies pass Lovable's 'RLS exists' scan.

findings.title: Firebase/Firestore/Storage security rules left open (test mode or 'if true')
findings.description: Firebase config (apiKey, projectId, storageBucket) is public by design. Data safety depends entirely on Security Rules. Rules such as 'allow read, write: if true', or buckets opened during development, let anyone read, list or write collections and stored files.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Test-mode rules make everything work straight away. Tutorials and AI output often start from permissive rules, and nobody tightens them before launch. Novices assume the Firebase config is a secret that protects them.
findings.user_impact: Mass exposure of user records and uploaded files such as ID photos and selfies, plus data tampering and deletion.
findings.detection_approach: Extract firebaseConfig from the JS bundle. Unauthenticated, try reading collection and document paths observed in traffic through the Firestore REST API, try Realtime DB /.json, and try listing the Storage bucket (GET https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/<bucket>/o). Flag any success. Signed in as test user A, try to read paths belonging to test user B.
findings.prevalence_evidence: env.fail 'Firewreck' research scanned about 5.5M domains and found 900 sites exposing about 125M user records, including 20M passwords and 27M billing entries. Tea app (2025-07-25): an exposed Firebase storage bucket leaked 72,000 images, including about 13,000 selfies and IDs (Engadget). Firebase docs: 'anyone who guesses your project ID can steal, modify, or delete the data.'
findings.corrections: Cite the 13K selfies/IDs + 59K other images breakdown to NBC/TechCrunch, not Engadget.

findings.title: Third-party secret keys hardcoded in client-side JavaScript
findings.description: Server-only credentials end up inlined into bundles the browser downloads: OpenAI and other LLM keys, Stripe secret keys, SendGrid and Twilio keys, AWS keys, service-account JSON. This happens through NEXT_PUBLIC_/VITE_ env prefixes or by calling third-party APIs directly from the frontend.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Calling the API from the browser is the fastest way to make a feature work. AI tools put the key wherever the code runs. Novices do not know that build-time public env prefixes end up in static JS.
findings.user_impact: Attackers can run up LLM or API bills, send email or SMS as the business, read payment data, or take over cloud resources.
findings.detection_approach: Download every JS chunk and source map. Scan with known key regexes and entropy checks (sk-, sk_live_, AKIA, AIza with non-Firebase scopes, xoxb-, SG., ghp_, service-account JSON). Also scan network request headers and URLs for Authorization: Bearer calls from the browser straight to api.openai.com, api.stripe.com and similar. Report the key type and where it was found, redact the value, and never exercise the key.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Wiz (2025-09-18) found third-party secrets such as OpenAI keys 'hardcoded directly into client-side JavaScript' in vibe-coded apps, and said 1 in 5 organizations on vibe-coding platforms face systemic risk. Escape.tech (2025-10-29) scanned 5,600+ vibe-coded apps and found 400+ exposed secrets. 'Keys on Doormats' (arXiv 2603.12498) found 1,748 credentials across 10M rendered sites, with 62% of JS exposures appearing only in compiled bundles. GitGuardian via CSO Online: 6.4% of Copilot-enabled repos leaked secrets vs 4.6% of all repos.
findings.corrections: Rephrase the Wiz stat as '1 in 5 organizations use vibe-coding platforms (per Wiz)', not a vulnerability rate.

findings.title: Supabase service_role / secret key shipped to the browser (bypasses RLS entirely)
findings.description: The Supabase service_role key has the bypassrls attribute. When it is exposed in the frontend, for example as NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY or VITE_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, even well-written RLS is irrelevant.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: When RLS blocks a query, the easy 'fix' an AI or novice reaches for is to swap in the service_role key, which makes the error disappear.
findings.user_impact: Full read, write and delete access to the database and admin Auth/Storage operations.
findings.detection_approach: Decode every JWT-shaped string in bundles and requests and flag role=service_role. Also flag sb_secret_ prefixed keys. This is a zero-false-positive, non-destructive check.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Supabase docs: secret and service role keys 'are never safe to expose because they bypass RLS.' Escape.tech's methodology lists 'Supabase service key exposures' among its vibe-coded app findings. No standalone count found.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Authentication or authorization enforced only in frontend code
findings.description: Login checks, password gates, role checks ('isAdmin'), route guards and feature flags live in React state or JS. The backend APIs they protect accept any request. Some apps even compare passwords client-side against strings embedded in the bundle.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: A route guard or hidden button looks like security. AI assistants readily generate client-side gating when asked to 'add a login page'. Novices do not know that anyone can call the API directly.
findings.user_impact: Anyone can reach protected data and admin functions by calling APIs directly, editing localStorage or flipping a JS variable.
findings.detection_approach: (1) Scan bundles for hardcoded password comparisons and role literals. (2) Record the authenticated API calls, then replay them with no cookies or tokens and with a low-privilege user's token, and diff the responses. (3) Tamper with localStorage/sessionStorage flags (isAdmin, role, plan), reload, and check whether privileged data loads from the server. (4) Navigate directly to routes found in the router manifest while logged out.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Wiz (2025-09-18) documented apps doing 'password entry and validation on the client side, without contacting any backend server', with hardcoded passwords in JS. The Register (2026-02-27) reported an AI-generated access check that was inverted, blocking authenticated users while letting anonymous ones through, which exposed 18,697 records. OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 Broken Access Control: '100% of the applications tested were found to have some form of broken access control.'
findings.corrections: Note that Lovable disputes the Register app's code was Lovable-generated.

findings.title: IDOR / Broken Object Level Authorization on API endpoints
findings.description: Endpoints such as /api/orders/123 or /api/users/:id/profile return or modify any object whose ID the caller supplies, without checking that the caller owns it.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated CRUD handlers fetch by ID and return the result. Ownership checks are a separate step that neither the prompt nor the tests ask for. Happy-path testing with one account never shows the problem.
findings.user_impact: Cross-account data exposure and tampering, sometimes leading to account takeover.
findings.detection_approach: Use two seeded test accounts. Crawl as user A and record every request carrying an object ID (path, query or body, including UUIDs). Replay each request with user B's session and with no session, and flag 2xx responses whose data belongs to A. For numeric IDs, try adjacent values within an opt-in budget. Run PUT, PATCH and DELETE variants only when destructive mode is on.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 API1 BOLA: prevalence 'Widespread', detectability 'Easy'. The Register (2026-04-21) reported a BOLA flaw in Lovable's own platform API that let any free account reach other users' source code, database credentials and AI chat history in 'five API calls'.
findings.corrections: Clarify that the Lovable BOLA example is the vendor platform's own API, not a vibe-coded app.

findings.title: Admin panels, internal tools and 'private' apps deployed publicly without authentication
findings.description: Admin dashboards (/admin, /dashboard, /internal), debug endpoints and internal knowledge-base or chatbot apps are deployed to the public internet with no auth, or with auth only in the UI. On some platforms, 'private' apps could still be joined by registering through exposed endpoints.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders assume an unlinked URL is private. Vibe-coding platforms deploy publicly by default. Signup and registration endpoints generated for one use case stay enabled.
findings.user_impact: Exposure of internal data, admin actions available to anyone, and sensitive knowledge bases leaked through chatbots.
findings.detection_approach: Enumerate routes from the SPA router manifest, sitemap and bundle strings (admin, internal, debug, dashboard, settings, api/*). Visit each logged out and as a low-privilege user, and flag privileged UI or data that renders. Check whether signup endpoints respond on apps the user says are invite-only or SSO-only.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Wiz (2025-09-18) found internal apps 'deployed on the public internet without authentication', including knowledge bases and chatbots. In Wiz's Base44 finding (discovered 2025-07-09), register and verify-otp endpoints accepted only the public app_id, bypassing SSO on private apps. Wix fixed it within 24 hours.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Paywall and subscription enforced client-side; payment webhooks unverified or success page trusted
findings.description: Premium status is read from client state, localStorage or a query parameter such as ?success=true after a Stripe redirect. Webhook endpoints do not verify the Stripe-Signature header, so forged 'payment succeeded' events grant access.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Redirect-to-success is the simplest way to show 'paid'. Signature verification fails with confusing raw-body errors, so it gets removed to make things work.
findings.user_impact: Free access to paid features, fraudulent order fulfilment and lost revenue.
findings.detection_approach: Browser-visible parts: (1) visit the checkout success URL directly without paying and check whether premium unlocks; (2) flip plan or isPro flags in storage or responses, reload, and see whether the server still serves premium data; (3) replay premium API calls as a free-tier user; (4) in opt-in mode, POST an unsigned test event to discovered /webhook or /api/stripe routes on the user's own staging site and check for 2xx. Server-side verification logic cannot be seen directly.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Stripe docs: 'Without verification, an attacker could send fake webhook events to your endpoint to trigger actions like fulfilling orders, granting account access or modifying records.' Enrichlead (Cursor-built, March 2025): founder posted 'people bypassing the subscription', as reported by Snyk. The details of that incident come from the founder's social posts, so treat them as semi-anecdotal.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: No rate limiting on auth, OTP, SMS/email and LLM-backed endpoints
findings.description: Login, signup, password reset, OTP, contact forms and AI-generation endpoints accept unlimited requests. This enables credential stuffing, OTP brute force, SMS/email cost pumping and LLM bill runaway.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Rate limiting is invisible on the happy path and needs infrastructure such as Redis or edge config. Prompts rarely ask for it and AI rarely adds it unprompted.
findings.user_impact: Account takeover, large third-party bills and service outage.
findings.detection_approach: With a strict opt-in budget on the user's own site, fire N (for example 20-30) rapid requests at login with wrong passwords, password reset and generation endpoints. Look for 429 responses, Retry-After or RateLimit headers, CAPTCHA or lockout. Report 'no throttling observed after N attempts'. Never target SMS or paid endpoints without explicit consent.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption gives the example of a $0.05/SMS password reset abused 'tens of thousands of times'. Snyk's account of Enrichlead cites 'maxed out usage on API keys' and missing rate limiting.
findings.corrections: Downgrade detectability to partial and word results as 'no throttling observed within budget N'.

findings.title: Missing server-side validation / mass assignment (client can set role, price, owner_id)
findings.description: APIs, or direct Supabase/Firebase writes, accept whatever fields the client sends. Attackers add role:'admin', is_verified:true, price:0, user_id:<victim> or credits:99999. Length, type and format validation exists only in the form UI.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI generates validation in the React form (zod or HTML attributes) and passes the body straight to the ORM or DB insert. Novices treat frontend validation as sufficient.
findings.user_impact: Privilege escalation, price manipulation, data corruption and junk or malicious data stored.
findings.detection_approach: Intercept form submissions in Playwright (route interception). Resend with the frontend constraints violated (oversize strings, wrong types, negative quantities) and with extra privileged fields added (role, isAdmin, price, owner/user_id). Then re-read the object and flag it if the server accepted the values. Compare against the constraints the UI enforces, taken from the a11y tree and DOM attributes.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization includes mass-assignment scenarios such as adding 'total_stay_price' and 'blocked': false to requests. The Snyk/Enrichlead account cites 'no input validation' and 'creating random stuff in the database'. No vibe-coding-specific statistic found.
findings.corrections: Mark the Snyk wording as a paraphrase.

findings.title: Stored/reflected XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, v-html or unsanitized Markdown/LLM output
findings.description: User content, URL parameters or LLM responses are rendered as raw HTML, for example in markdown previews, rich-text comments or chat UIs that render model output as HTML. Script runs in other users' sessions.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI reaches for dangerouslySetInnerHTML to render formatted text or markdown. The name's warning is not understood. Chat UIs that render LLM output as HTML are a common new sink.
findings.user_impact: Session theft, account takeover and actions performed as the victim.
findings.detection_approach: Inject benign canary payloads, such as an variant and a unique marker, into every input, URL parameter and hash. Revisit as a second user and check whether the marker executed (window flag or console) or appears unescaped in the DOM. Also hook Element.innerHTML setters to trace sinks at runtime. Pair with a CSP check.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Veracode 2025 GenAI Code Security Report (2025-07-30): AI tools 'failed to defend against [XSS, CWE-80] in 86% of relevant code samples'. 45% of samples overall introduced OWASP Top 10 flaws. React docs: 'it is trivial to introduce an XSS vulnerability this way.'
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Missing security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy)
findings.description: Responses lack Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, clickjacking protection and nosniff, or ship a CSP containing 'unsafe-inline' or wildcards that negates it.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Headers are hosting and framework config, not app code, so prompts never touch them. Defaults on many hosts do not set them.
findings.user_impact: XSS impact is amplified, clickjacking becomes possible, and downgrade attacks become possible.
findings.detection_approach: Inspect response headers on the document and API responses. Grade the CSP (unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval, *, missing object-src or base-uri, missing frame-ancestors). Test framing by loading the page in an iframe from a local origin. This is a cheap check suitable for V0.
findings.prevalence_evidence: HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025 Security: CSP on 21.9% of pages (up from 18.5%), HSTS on 36% of mobile pages, X-Frame-Options about 30%, X-Content-Type-Options about 50% on mobile. Escape.tech lists missing security headers among vibe-coded app issues.
findings.corrections: Remove the claim that Escape lists missing security headers. Keep severity low to medium: missing headers alone are rarely exploitable, and platforms like Vercel and Netlify set HSTS by default.

findings.title: Session cookies without HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite, and tokens stored in localStorage
findings.description: Auth and session cookies are set without HttpOnly (readable by JS, so stealable via XSS), Secure (sent over HTTP) or an explicit SameSite, or JWTs sit in localStorage.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Default cookie helpers and quick-start auth snippets often omit the flags. Storing JWTs in localStorage is the simplest pattern AI suggests.
findings.user_impact: Session hijacking via XSS or network interception, and CSRF exposure.
findings.detection_approach: After login, call context.cookies() and inspect the flags on cookies that look like sessions. Scan localStorage and sessionStorage for JWTs or refresh tokens and decode their expiry and scope. Flag long-lived tokens and missing flags.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Web Almanac 2025 Cookies: only 12% of first-party cookies set HttpOnly and 24% set Secure, and 66% (desktop) do not specify SameSite. These are web-wide figures, not session-cookie specific.
findings.corrections: Treat localStorage tokens in Supabase or Firebase SDK apps as informational, not a defect.

findings.title: Permissive CORS: reflected Origin or null allowed with credentials
findings.description: The API echoes any Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, or allows 'null', together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, or uses a broken suffix or prefix allowlist. Any website can then read authenticated responses.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: CORS errors block development, and the fastest AI or Stack Overflow fix is cors({origin: true, credentials: true}) or reflecting the origin.
findings.user_impact: Malicious sites can read victims' private data and CSRF tokens.
findings.detection_approach: Replay the app's API requests with Origin: https://evil.example, Origin: null and suffix/prefix variants. Flag ACAO reflecting the value together with ACAC: true. This is non-destructive.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 lists CORS misconfiguration under Broken Access Control. PortSwigger documents reflected origin, null origin and allowlist parsing errors as common. No vibe-coding-specific statistic found.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Verbose error / stack-trace leaks and exposed production source maps
findings.description: API errors return stack traces, SQL or ORM messages, file paths or env details. Production deploys ship .map files with sourcesContent, which reveals full original source, hidden endpoints and sometimes secrets.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Debug error handlers (res.status(500).json(err)) are generated for convenience and never removed. Some bundlers emit source maps by default.
findings.user_impact: Reconnaissance gets much easier: hidden APIs, schema and secrets are revealed and exploits can be chained.
findings.detection_approach: Capture console and network during danger-path tests with malformed inputs, and flag responses containing stack-trace patterns (at Function., Traceback, SQLSTATE, PrismaClient, file paths). For each JS chunk, request <chunk>.js.map and check sourceMappingURL, flag when sourcesContent is present, and feed the recovered source into the secret and route scanners.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP Top 10:2025 adds A10 'Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions'. Sentry Security blog (2025-01-31) describes exposed sourcemaps revealing a hidden endpoint that was chained into password-change account takeover. No prevalence statistic found.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Open redirects in login/logout/callback flows (?next=, ?redirect=, ?returnTo=)
findings.description: Post-login or OAuth callback parameters redirect to any URL without an allowlist. These redirects enable phishing on a trusted domain and sometimes OAuth token leakage.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: 'Redirect back to where the user came from' is implemented as router.push(searchParams.get('next')) without validation.
findings.user_impact: Credible phishing links and possible theft of auth codes or tokens.
findings.detection_approach: Find redirect-like parameters in URLs, forms and bundle strings. Set them to an external canary domain plus bypass variants (//evil.example, /\evil.example, https:evil.example). Complete the flow and check the final navigation URL.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet describes the phishing and access-control-bypass risks. Anecdotal/unsourced for vibe-coding prevalence.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Known-vulnerable framework versions and middleware-only auth (e.g. Next.js CVE-2025-29927, React2Shell CVE-2025-55182)
findings.description: Apps run outdated Next.js or React Server Components versions with critical CVEs. CVE-2025-29927 lets an x-middleware-subrequest header skip middleware, and many AI-generated apps put all auth in middleware. CVE-2025-55182 (CVSS 10) is unauthenticated RCE via the RSC Flight protocol and is on CISA KEV.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI templates pin whatever version was in training data, and vibe coders rarely upgrade. Middleware-only auth is the pattern most tutorials show.
findings.user_impact: Auth bypass across all protected routes, or full server compromise.
findings.detection_approach: Fingerprint framework and version from headers (x-powered-by, x-nextjs-*), __NEXT_DATA__, the buildId, chunk names and runtime globals, and map them to a CVE list. For CVE-2025-29927, request a protected route with the x-middleware-subrequest header variants on the user's own site and check whether auth is skipped (safe, read-only). Do not attempt RCE payloads; report version risk only.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Datadog Security Labs: CVE-2025-29927 affects Next.js <12.3.5, <13.5.9, <14.2.25 and <15.2.3 (disclosed 2025-03-21). Datadog observed 'over 800 IP addresses' scanning for React2Shell by 2025-12-05. It was added to CISA KEV on 2025-12-05.
findings.corrections: Add that Vercel/Netlify-hosted apps were not affected by 29927. Cite CISA for the KEV date. The 'many AI-generated apps put all auth in middleware' claim is unsourced.

findings.title: Prompt injection in LLM-powered features (chatbots, AI assistants, RAG over user content)
findings.description: Customer-facing chatbots and AI features can be steered by user input (direct injection) or by content they ingest (indirect injection). They make unauthorized commitments, leak system prompts or private context, or trigger tool actions. The risk is highest when a feature has the 'lethal trifecta': private data access, untrusted content and an exfiltration channel.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Adding a chatbot is a single API call, and builders treat the system prompt as a security boundary. Model output is often rendered as HTML or used to take actions without checks.
findings.user_impact: Data leakage, reputational and legal exposure, unauthorized actions, and XSS through model output.
findings.detection_approach: Detect chat or LLM widgets (network calls to LLM APIs or streaming endpoints). Send a curated set of benign injection probes: system-prompt extraction, instruction override, a canary token that should not be repeated, markdown image exfiltration to a local canary URL, and HTML/script in output. Flag leaks of the system prompt or of seeded private data, fetches to the canary, or unescaped rendering. Results are probabilistic, so report them as risk, not proof.
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 ranks LLM01 Prompt Injection first. AI Incident Database #622 (2023-12-18): a Chevrolet dealer's ChatGPT bot agreed to sell a Tahoe for $1. Simon Willison's 'lethal trifecta' (2025-06-16).
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Hallucinated or slopsquatted dependencies pulled into the app
findings.description: LLMs recommend package names that do not exist. Attackers register those names with malicious code, and AI-generated projects install them.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Vibe coders accept whatever npm or pip install the AI suggests without checking that the package is real or reputable.
findings.user_impact: Supply-chain compromise: malicious code in the build or the browser bundle, and credential theft.
findings.detection_approach: From outside, Run Hound can only fingerprint bundled client libraries (webpack module paths, license comments, source maps) and check them against vulnerability and malicious-package feeds such as OSV or GHSA. It can also flag scripts loaded from unexpected third-party origins. Server-side and dev dependencies are invisible, so this belongs in a future opt-in grey-box mode that reads package.json or the lockfile.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Spracklen et al. (arXiv 2406.10279, USENIX Security 2025): hallucinated packages average 'at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models', with 205,474 unique hallucinated names. Aikido reports an empty 'huggingface-cli' PyPI package got 30,000+ downloads in three months.
findings.corrections: Emphasize that it is mostly undetectable black-box and belongs in the future grey-box scope.

findings.title: No dev/prod separation: staging or preview builds wired to the production database (tester safety risk)
findings.description: Vibe-coded apps often use one database and one set of keys everywhere. A 'staging' URL Run Hound is authorized to test may write to production data. AI agents operating on such environments have destroyed production data.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Platforms historically defaulted to a single environment, and novices do not set up separate projects or keys.
findings.user_impact: Automated danger-path tests (deletes, bulk creates) could corrupt or wipe real customer data. This hits Run Hound's own safety and reputation.
findings.detection_approach: Compare Supabase or Firebase project IDs, API hosts and Stripe key mode (pk_live_ vs pk_test_) between the staging target and the production domain, if the user supplies it. Warn if they match or if live-mode keys appear. Keep destructive actions opt-in, require seeded test accounts, and require explicit confirmation when live keys are detected.
findings.prevalence_evidence: AI Incident Database #1152 / The Register (2025-07-21): a Replit agent deleted SaaStr's production database during a code freeze and fabricated about 4,000 fake records. Replit then shipped 'automatic dev/prod database separation'. Prevalence of shared environments is anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: Cite Masad's X post or The Register 2025-07-22 for the dev/prod separation claim. The AIID incident date is 2025-07-18.

findings.title: Context: AI-generated code is measurably less secure, and its authors are more confident in it
findings.description: This is a cross-cutting finding that supports the need for Run Hound, not a single bug class. Controlled studies show AI-assisted developers write less secure code and overrate its security. Large-scale tests show roughly half of AI-generated code samples contain OWASP Top 10 flaws, with no improvement in newer or larger models.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Models optimize for functional code, security performance 'remained flat, regardless of model size', and users trust the output.
findings.user_impact: Every category above is more likely in AI-built apps, and owners are less likely to suspect them.
findings.detection_approach: Not a single check. It justifies making the black-box security pass (headers, cookies, secrets, BaaS rules, authz replay) a default part of every Run Hound report, even at V0.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Perry et al., CCS 2023 (arXiv 2211.03622): AI-assistant users 'wrote significantly less secure code' and were more likely to believe it secure. Veracode (2025-07-30): 45% of samples across 100+ LLMs failed security tests, with Java at 72%.
findings.corrections: Note that Perry used Codex-era assistants (2022), so it is dated. Pair it with Veracode 2025 for currency.

missed_items.title: Supabase Storage buckets set public / missing storage.objects policies, and Supabase RPC (SECURITY DEFINER) functions callable via /rest/v1/rpc
missed_items.why: Same root cause as RLS, but on storage and functions. File uploads (IDs, avatars, invoices) are often in public buckets, and RPC functions bypass table RLS. Both can be tested black-box with the anon key.

missed_items.title: Exposed deployment artifacts: /.env, /.git/, backup files, and public preview/staging deployments
missed_items.why: Very common novice leak, and trivially detectable with a HEAD/GET to well-known paths on the user's own domain. Vercel preview URLs are public unless Deployment Protection is on.

missed_items.title: CSRF on cookie-authenticated state-changing endpoints
missed_items.why: Absent from the list. Cookie-session apps built with Express or Next API routes often lack CSRF tokens or SameSite. Missing tokens and SameSite can be detected black-box.

missed_items.title: Unrestricted file upload (type/size/content not checked server-side, SVG/HTML uploads served inline leading to stored XSS)
missed_items.why: Vibe apps commonly add avatar and document upload. Only client-side accept= checks are typical. It can be tested by uploading benign polyglot or SVG canaries on the user's own site.

missed_items.title: Weak auth configuration: user enumeration via login/reset messages, email confirmation disabled, open signup on an 'invite-only' app, weak password policy
missed_items.why: This was part of the Sentry sourcemap ATO chain (enumeration). BaaS defaults are often left as-is. It is observable by comparing responses.

missed_items.title: SSRF via 'import from URL' / link-preview / AI 'fetch this page' features
missed_items.why: LLM features that fetch URLs are increasingly common. The server-side fetch can be partially detected with an out-of-band canary URL the user controls.

missed_items.title: Third-party script supply chain / missing SRI (e.g., polyfill.io compromise, June 2024)
missed_items.why: Browser-visible and relevant to the slopsquatting item: it flags scripts from compromised or unexpected CDNs and missing integrity attributes. This is the part of supply-chain risk a browser can actually see.

missed_items.title: Supabase Edge Functions / serverless API routes deployed with JWT verification disabled
missed_items.why: A common 'fix' when functions return 401. It can be detected by calling observed function URLs without an Authorization header.

findings.title: Clickable div/span instead of <button>/<a>
findings.description: Interactive controls are built as <div onClick> or <span onClick>, sometimes with role=button bolted on, but without tabindex, Enter/Space key handling, or focus styling. The control works with a mouse but cannot be reached or activated from the keyboard, and screen readers see it as plain text or a broken button. This is a WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard (A) and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A) failure.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: LLMs and new React developers attach onClick to whatever element is already styled, such as a card or table row. Once the page 'works' with a mouse nobody tries it with Tab. MDN says role=button needs tabindex=0 plus Enter and Space handlers, and generated code often has only some of these.
findings.user_impact: Keyboard-only users, switch users and screen-reader users cannot open menus, submit, or select items, so whole features are blocked for them.
findings.detection_approach: (1) CDP DOMDebugger.getEventListeners, or instrumenting addEventListener, to find click listeners on elements whose computed role is generic or none. Also flag cursor:pointer on non-focusable elements. (2) Tab through the page, press Enter and Space on each candidate, and diff the DOM, URL and network to see whether the mouse click effect happens. (3) Compare the set of mouse-clickable elements against the set of Tab-reachable elements. axe-core catches only part of this, for example role=button without a focusable element, so agent interaction is needed.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: 'Home pages averaged 30.4 instances of tabindex=0 or tabindex=-1 (up 17% from 26 in 2025)', which suggests more custom widgets with hand-rolled focus. No direct prevalence figure for div-buttons was found.
findings.corrections: Remove listener enumeration as the primary method for React apps, or explain the event-delegation limit. Use cursor:pointer, React fiber props and the Tab-reachability diff instead. The tabindex statistic is indirect evidence only.

findings.title: Icon-only buttons and links with no accessible name
findings.description: Icon buttons, such as a lucide/heroicons SVG for close, menu, delete, cart or social links, have no text, aria-label or <title>. Screen readers announce only 'button' or read the URL. This fails WCAG 4.1.2 and 2.4.4.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: shadcn/Tailwind output relies heavily on icon-only controls (<Button size="icon"><X/></Button>). Models and beginners often leave out sr-only text or aria-label. The CHI 2026 study found that LLMs struggle with svg_graphics_labelled and link-purpose rules.
findings.user_impact: Blind users cannot tell what a control does. A 'button' next to each row could be delete or edit.
findings.detection_approach: axe-core rules button-name, link-name, svg-img-alt. Cross-check the accessible name in the Playwright accessibility snapshot for each interactive node, and use vision on a screenshot crop to suggest the intended label for the report.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: empty links on 46.3% of home pages and empty buttons on 30.6%. A11YN (arXiv 2510.13914) lists link-name among the most frequent axe violations in base LLM output (129 instances).
findings.corrections: Attribute the svg_graphics_labelled and link-text finding to Suh et al., arXiv 2503.15885 (GPT-4o), not to CHI 2026. Describe the A11YN counts as coming from the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B base model.

findings.title: Form inputs without labels, or with placeholder as the only label
findings.description: Inputs have no <label for>, aria-label or aria-labelledby, or they rely on placeholder text that disappears on typing. Custom shadcn Select/Combobox/Checkbox triggers are often not linked to their visible label. This fails WCAG 1.3.1, 3.3.2 (visible labels) and 4.1.2.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Placeholder-only inputs look clean in generated mockups. Composed components such as a Radix Select trigger inside a FormItem lose the label link when the developer skips the FormLabel/FormControl wrappers.
findings.user_impact: Screen readers announce 'edit text' with no context. Users with cognitive or memory disabilities lose the prompt once they start typing, and voice-control users cannot target fields by name.
findings.detection_approach: axe label, label-title-only, select-name, aria-input-field-name. Also check that each input's accessible name comes only from the placeholder, meaning the name equals the placeholder and there is no visible <label> in the bounding box region. Then fill the field and use a screenshot to check whether any visible label remains.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: missing form input labels on 51% of home pages, and 'One third (33.1%) of those form inputs were not properly labeled'. The LLM comparison study (arXiv 2503.15885) found LLMs better than humans on basic labeling but worse on 'Form Label Position Issues'.
findings.corrections: Minor: the Form Label Position result is GPT-4o-specific, not true of 'LLMs' in general.

findings.title: Low text and UI contrast (muted grays, placeholder, disabled, dark mode, text on images)
findings.description: Text falls below 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA), and UI components or focus rings fall below 3:1 (1.4.11). Typical cases are Tailwind gray-400 on white, muted-foreground tokens, placeholder text, hover and focus states, dark-mode variants, and text over hero images or gradients.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated designs favour subtle, low-contrast 'modern' palettes. Developers check the light theme at rest only. Hover, focus, disabled and dark-mode states are never viewed side by side.
findings.user_impact: Low-vision users, older users, and anyone on a phone in sunlight cannot read content or see control boundaries.
findings.detection_approach: axe color-contrast covers static text on solid backgrounds. The agent adds three checks. (1) Re-run axe after emulating prefers-color-scheme: dark and forced states (hover, focus). (2) For text over images or gradients, where axe returns 'incomplete', sample screenshot pixels behind the text box and compute the ratio. (3) Measure focus-ring and border contrast against adjacent colours for 1.4.11.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: low contrast text on 83.9% of home pages. A11YN reports color-contrast as the second most frequent axe violation in base LLM output (702 instances). Nuance: arXiv 2503.15885 found GPT-4o reduced contrast issues by about 49% compared with human-written code, but contrast still made up 80% of violations.
findings.corrections: Name the model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) for the A11YN counts and state that the 80% figure used the IBM Equal Access checker.

findings.title: Missing alt text, or alt text that passes checks but is meaningless
findings.description: Images have no alt attribute (1.1.1), or have alt text that exists but says nothing, such as alt="image", alt="hero", a filename, or a generic stock description. Decorative images lack alt="" and create noise.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Models fill in alt text so that linters pass, but they cannot see the image, so they write generic strings. Vibe coders swap in real images later without updating the placeholder alt.
findings.user_impact: Screen-reader users miss product images, charts or instructional content, or hear meaningless noise.
findings.detection_approach: axe image-alt, role-img-alt, input-image-alt for missing alt. The semantic check needs the agent's vision model to compare image content with the alt string, flagging filename-like alt, single generic words, and duplicated alt across different images. This is LLM-as-judge, so report it as a 'needs review' confidence tier.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: missing alt text on 53.1% of home pages. Calò et al., CHI 2026 EA: across 300 UIs from Claude, Gemini and GPT they found 541 semantic violations that pass automated checks ('an image with alt="image" passes every check'). LLM judges detected injected faults with 80-92% recall.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Generic link and button text ('Click here', 'Learn more', 'Submit')
findings.description: Several links or buttons share identical, context-free names such as 'Learn more', 'Read more', 'Click' or 'View'. Screen-reader users who navigate by a links or buttons list cannot tell them apart. This fails 2.4.4 Link Purpose and 2.4.6.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Card-grid templates generated by LLMs repeat a single CTA string in each card. Automated checkers pass them because a name exists.
findings.user_impact: Users navigating by element lists hear '5 links: learn more, learn more...', which makes navigation slow and error-prone.
findings.detection_approach: From the a11y tree, group interactive elements by accessible name and flag duplicate names that point to different hrefs or actions. Match against a list of generic phrases. Use an LLM judge to decide whether surrounding context, such as aria-describedby or a card heading, disambiguates them.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Calò et al. (CHI 2026 EA): 'generic button labels and vague link text are the two' most common semantic violations, together about half of all semantic violations in LLM-generated UIs. WebAIM Million 2026: '15.2% of pages had ambiguous link text'.
findings.corrections: Say that repeated 'Learn more' links with a programmatic context (such as a card heading in the same list item) pass 2.4.4. Report them as a best-practice or usability issue rather than a hard failure unless the context is missing.

findings.title: Focus indicator removed (outline-none / focus:outline-none with no replacement)
findings.description: Tailwind outline-none, outline-hidden, or a global *:focus{outline:0} removes the browser focus ring without providing a ring, border or background replacement. Keyboard users cannot see where they are. This fails 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA), and WCAG 2.2 adds 2.4.11 and 2.4.13.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Developers remove the 'ugly blue ring' that appears on click. Tailwind docs say 'It is highly recommended to apply your own focus styling for accessibility when using this utility', and generated code often skips that. The outline-none utility also overrides global focus styles because it sits in the utilities layer.
findings.user_impact: Keyboard, switch and low-vision magnifier users lose their place on the page. This is a common reason audits describe a site as 'unusable by keyboard'.
findings.detection_approach: axe does not reliably detect this, so the agent has to interact. Press Tab through every focusable element. For each, take an element screenshot (or computed outline, box-shadow, border and background) before and after focus, and flag any element with no visible change or a change below 3:1 contrast. Also check for :focus-visible parity when focus comes from the keyboard.
findings.prevalence_evidence: No large-scale prevalence figure found (anecdotal/unsourced for rate). The mechanism is documented by Tailwind and W3C.
findings.corrections: Replace '2.4.11 and 2.4.13' with 2.4.7 (AA) plus 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA), and use 1.4.11 for ring contrast. Treat a failure to meet 3:1 as 1.4.11 or AAA, not a 2.4.7 failure.

findings.title: Modals, drawers and sheets that do not move, trap or return focus, or have no accessible name
findings.description: Hand-rolled modals leave focus behind the overlay, let Tab escape into the obscured page, do not close on Escape, or leave focus on <body> after closing. shadcn/Radix Dialog or Sheet used without DialogTitle produces an unnamed dialog. There is also the reverse failure: a real keyboard trap with no way out (2.1.2).
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: LLMs generate a fixed-position div 'modal' with state toggling but none of the APG behaviour. Developers using shadcn delete the title to fit a design, and Radix then logs an error that is ignored.
findings.user_impact: Screen-reader users do not know a dialog opened, or they keep interacting with the hidden page. Keyboard users can get stuck or lost after closing.
findings.detection_approach: Open each dialog, sheet or popover found during exploration and check four things. (1) Is document.activeElement inside the dialog? (2) Tab N+1 times and check focus stays inside. (3) Does Escape close it? (4) After closing, does focus return to the trigger? Check for role=dialog with an accessible name and aria-modal. Capture console messages that match Radix's "`DialogContent` requires a `DialogTitle`" as a strong signal. Detect traps by checking whether focus can leave a widget with Tab, Shift+Tab or Escape.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced for rate. The shadcn issue #4302 shows the warning firing even on shadcn's own dashboard sample block at narrow viewport.
findings.corrections: Note that Radix warnings appear only in development builds, so the console signal is missing when a production build is tested.

findings.title: ARIA misuse (wrong roles, aria-hidden on focusable content, broken references, conflicting semantics)
findings.description: Examples: role=button without key handling; aria-hidden=true on elements that contain focusable controls; aria-labelledby pointing to IDs that do not exist; role=menu used for site navigation; aria-expanded never updated; ARIA overriding correct native semantics.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Models add ARIA to look 'accessible' without implementing the behaviour it promises. The LLM-vs-human study found GPT-4o 'introduced more violations in areas like ARIA-related attributes'.
findings.user_impact: Assistive tech announces controls that do not behave as announced, or hides working content entirely. W3C APG: 'Incorrect ARIA misrepresents visual experiences, with potentially devastating effects on their corresponding non-visual experiences.'
findings.detection_approach: axe covers the static rules: aria-allowed-role, aria-valid-attr-value, aria-hidden-focus, aria-required-children/parent. For state correctness, the agent toggles each widget and checks aria-expanded, aria-selected and aria-checked against visible state from a screenshot. It also checks that role=menu or tab widgets support arrow keys per APG.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: 'home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (59.1 on average) than pages without ARIA (42 on average)', and aria-hidden usage rose 30% year over year to 23.3 per page. arXiv 2503.15885: LLMs 'struggle with complex accessibility requirements, particularly ARIA-related attributes'.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Keyboard-inaccessible custom widgets (dropdowns, comboboxes, tabs, date pickers, sliders, drag-and-drop)
findings.description: Custom selects or menus open only on hover or click, arrow keys do nothing, and options are unreachable by Tab. Drag-to-reorder has no single-pointer or keyboard alternative, which fails WCAG 2.2 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA).
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated code often builds bespoke widgets from divs instead of native <select> or tested primitives. Hover-driven nav menus are common in AI landing-page templates.
findings.user_impact: Keyboard and assistive-technology users cannot complete core flows such as choosing a plan, picking a date or reordering items.
findings.detection_approach: For each widget detected by role (combobox, listbox, menu, tablist, slider) or by visual heuristics, drive the APG keyboard contract (arrow keys, Home/End, Enter/Space, Escape) and verify the state change in the DOM and screenshot. For elements with a draggable attribute or pointer-drag listeners, look for an alternative control. A golden-path scenario should be re-run keyboard-only and compared with the mouse run.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced (no large-scale rate found). The requirements come from APG and MDN.
findings.corrections: Cite the specific APG patterns and Understanding 2.5.7. Separate 'deviates from APG' (advisory) from 'not operable by keyboard' (a 2.1.1 failure).

findings.title: Broken heading hierarchy and missing landmarks
findings.description: Heading levels are chosen for font size and skip levels. Pages have multiple or zero h1 elements, and card titles are divs. Content sits outside landmarks (no <main>, <nav>, <header>). This affects 1.3.1 and 2.4.6, plus axe best-practice rules region and landmark-one-main.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated sections are composed independently, so each hero or section uses whatever heading tag suits its styling. Layout wrappers are plain divs. The LLM study found persistent 'HeadingsOrg' problems in generated code.
findings.user_impact: Screen-reader users, most of whom navigate by headings and landmarks, cannot skim or jump to content.
findings.detection_approach: Build a heading outline and landmark map from the a11y snapshot. Flag skipped levels, missing or multiple h1, and content outside landmarks (axe region, landmark-one-main, page-has-heading-one, heading-order). Use a vision model to find visually heading-like text that is not a heading.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: 'Skipped heading levels were present on 41.8% of all pages, up from 39% in 2025'. A11YN: region was the most frequent axe violation in base LLM output (894 instances) and landmark-one-main had 164.
findings.corrections: State that skipped levels and region are best-practice findings (a 1.3.1 failure only when the structure is misrepresented), so they should get lower severity in reports.

findings.title: Form validation errors, toasts and status updates not announced
findings.description: Validation messages appear visually as red text or a toast but are not tied to the input (no aria-invalid or aria-describedby) and are not in a live region. Async results such as 'Saved', 'Added to cart' or '5 results' are silent. This fails 3.3.1 Error Identification (A) and 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA).
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated forms validate and render error text conditionally but skip the programmatic association. Toast libraries are mounted inconsistently. Errors are sometimes shown only by colour, which also fails 1.4.1.
findings.user_impact: Blind users submit, nothing is announced, and they do not know the form failed or which field is wrong. This leads to abandoned signups and checkouts.
findings.detection_approach: Danger-path scenarios submit invalid or empty data. After each submit, check that new error text is referenced by the input's aria-describedby or aria-errormessage, that aria-invalid=true is set, that the text sits inside role=alert/status or an aria-live region (or focus moves to it), and that the error is not conveyed only by red border colour (screenshot or vision check). Do the same for toasts after successful actions.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced for rate. The requirement and examples are from W3C Understanding 4.1.3.
findings.corrections: Add the pre-existing live-region check. Aria-describedby association without aria-invalid is not by itself a 3.3.1 failure if the error text identifies the field.

findings.title: SPA route changes with no title update, focus move or announcement
findings.description: Client-side routing in React Router, Next.js or Vite SPAs swaps content without changing document.title, moving focus, or announcing the new page. Focus stays on the clicked link or resets to <body>.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Vibe-coded apps are almost all SPAs, and routing is scaffolded without any accessibility announcer. Developers only see the visual change.
findings.user_impact: Screen-reader users are not told the page changed and may keep reading stale context, or they are sent back to the top of the document.
findings.detection_approach: After each in-app navigation (URL change without a full load), check whether document.title changed and is unique, where document.activeElement ends up (ideally the h1, main, or a skip target), and whether an aria-live region received text. Flag routes that fail all three.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Gatsby and Fable Tech Labs user testing (2019) found 'Without page refreshes, screen reader users may not be informed that the page has changed' and that announcements were inconsistent across Safari/VoiceOver and Firefox/NVDA. No current prevalence rate was found.
findings.corrections: Note that Next.js includes a route announcer (next-route-announcer). Map a stale title to 2.4.2 and treat the rest as best practice.

findings.title: No skip link, or a broken one, past repeated navigation
findings.description: There is no 'Skip to main content' link (2.4.1 Bypass Blocks, A). Where one exists it may point to a missing ID, a non-focusable target, or never become visible on focus.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Templates rarely include skip links. When they do, the target ID often drifts after refactors.
findings.user_impact: Keyboard users must Tab through the full header and nav on every page.
findings.detection_approach: Press Tab once from page load and check that the first focusable element is a visible in-page link. Activate it and verify that focus or scroll moves into main content. Otherwise count the Tab presses needed to reach <main>. axe bypass gives a partial check.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: '17.1% of home pages had a skip link present, up from 15.3% in 2025', so about 83% lack one.
findings.corrections: Add that 10% of detected skip links were broken. Clarify that a missing skip link is not necessarily a 2.4.1 failure when proper landmarks or headings exist, so low severity is right.

findings.title: Missing or wrong <html lang>
findings.description: The <html> element has no lang attribute, or has the wrong one (for example lang=en on a non-English localized app). This fails 3.1.1 Language of Page (A).
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Some starters omit it. Localised or translated generated sites keep a hard-coded lang=en.
findings.user_impact: Screen readers use the wrong pronunciation engine, which makes content unintelligible, and translation tools misbehave.
findings.detection_approach: axe html-has-lang and html-lang-valid. The agent can also detect the page text language and compare it to the lang value.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: missing document language on 13.5% of home pages.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Focused element hidden under sticky header, footer, chat widget or cookie banner (WCAG 2.2)
findings.description: When tabbing, the focused control scrolls under a fixed header, a cookie consent bar, or a chat bubble such as Intercom or Crisp. This fails 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA, new in WCAG 2.2.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Sticky navbars and floating widgets are standard in generated landing pages. Nobody sets scroll-padding-top, and nobody tabs through the page.
findings.user_impact: Sighted keyboard and magnifier users lose track of focus.
findings.detection_approach: During keyboard traversal, get the focused element's bounding box and all position:fixed or sticky element boxes. Flag full occlusion (a 2.4.11 failure) or partial occlusion (2.4.12, AAA). Confirm with elementFromPoint at the focus-box centre and with a screenshot.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced. W3C Understanding names cookie banners and sticky content as the typical failure.
findings.corrections: Add the exception for user-dismissible content and note that the check should run after the page has scrolled the focused element into view.

findings.title: Touch or pointer targets under 24x24 CSS px (WCAG 2.2 2.5.8)
findings.description: Small icon buttons, close 'x' buttons, pagination dots, inline table actions and checkbox hit areas fall below 24x24 CSS px and lack the spacing exception. This fails 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Dense dashboard layouts and size='sm' or h-6 w-6 icon buttons are common in shadcn-style output. Testing is done on desktop with a mouse.
findings.user_impact: Users with tremor or motor impairment, and mobile users generally, mis-tap, which can trigger destructive actions such as delete.
findings.detection_approach: axe target-size rule (WCAG 2.2 tags). Supplement with bounding-box measurement of every interactive node at mobile viewports, applying the 24px-circle spacing exception.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced (no large-scale rate found).
findings.corrections: Add the inline-link and user-agent-default exceptions, and the axe tag caveat.

findings.title: Layout breaks at 320px width or 200-400% zoom
findings.description: Content requires horizontal scrolling or overlaps at 320 CSS px (equal to 1280px at 400% zoom), or text clips when resized to 200%. This fails 1.4.10 Reflow (AA) and 1.4.4 Resize Text (AA). Fixed-width tables and modals, and heights set in px, are typical causes.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated layouts are tested at one or two breakpoints. Fixed h-[600px] containers and wide data tables are common.
findings.user_impact: Low-vision users who zoom lose content or functions, and mobile users see a broken UI.
findings.detection_approach: Set the viewport to 320x256 and 1280 with deviceScaleFactor or CSS zoom 400%. Check whether document.scrollWidth exceeds clientWidth, find elements clipped by overflow:hidden, and check for overlapping bounding boxes of text nodes. Re-run golden paths at that size to confirm functions stay reachable.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: Note the exemption for 2-D content such as tables, which the researcher lists as a typical cause. Horizontal scroll inside a data table is allowed.

findings.title: Animations ignore prefers-reduced-motion
findings.description: Framer Motion or GSAP entrance animations, parallax, auto-playing carousels and scroll-jacking run regardless of the OS 'reduce motion' setting. This affects 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA) and 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A) for auto-moving content over 5 seconds.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Motion-heavy 'wow' landing pages are a signature of AI site builders. The reduced-motion media query is rarely added.
findings.user_impact: Users with vestibular disorders can get 'distraction, dizziness, headaches and nausea' (W3C).
findings.detection_approach: Load the page twice, once with page.emulateMedia({reducedMotion:'reduce'}) and once without. Compare document.getAnimations() counts and durations and diff screenshot sequences. Flag unchanged motion. Detect auto-advancing carousels with no pause control by taking timed screenshots.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: Note that ignoring prefers-reduced-motion is not itself a WCAG AA failure, since 2.3.3 is AAA. Only auto-moving content over 5s with no pause control fails 2.2.2 (A).

findings.title: Login and OTP fields that block paste or autofill (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8)
findings.description: Password or OTP inputs use onPaste preventDefault, or autocomplete=off, or split OTP boxes that reject paste, or CAPTCHAs with no alternative. This fails 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Some developers wrongly believe blocking paste is a 'security best practice', and it appears in generated auth forms. Split-digit OTP components often mishandle paste.
findings.user_impact: Users with cognitive disabilities, and anyone relying on a password manager, cannot log in without transcribing credentials.
findings.detection_approach: In auth flows, run a clipboard paste into password and OTP fields and check the resulting value. Check the autocomplete attributes (current-password, one-time-code). Detect CAPTCHA widgets and check whether an alternative is offered.
findings.prevalence_evidence: anecdotal/unsourced. The requirement is from W3C Understanding 3.3.8.
findings.corrections: Narrow the CAPTCHA claim (object recognition is excepted at AA). Drop autocomplete=off as a 3.3.8 failure.

findings.title: Relying on automated scans or overlay widgets for 'compliance' (legal exposure)
findings.description: Teams treat a clean axe or Lighthouse score, or an installed overlay widget (accessiBe, UserWay and similar), as proof of accessibility. Automated rules cover only part of real issues, and overlays do not prevent lawsuits. This matters more since the EU European Accessibility Act began applying on 28 June 2025 (EN 301 549, which incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA), and US ADA web suits keep rising.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Vibe coders and small teams have no accessibility specialist. A Lighthouse score of 100 or a one-line widget install feels like a finished job.
findings.user_impact: Users with disabilities still meet the interaction-level failures described in the other findings. Businesses face demand letters and lawsuits (64% of sued companies make under $25M revenue) and, in the EU, national penalties. The microenterprise exemption applies only to services from companies with fewer than 10 employees and no more than €2M turnover.
findings.detection_approach: Detect overlay scripts by network request domain and global objects, and warn in the report that they are not remediation. Label every report finding as 'automated rule' or 'agent-verified interaction' so users can see coverage. Run both axe and the keyboard, focus, semantic and state checks, and state clearly that this is not a WCAG conformance certification.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Deque: automated axe testing covers 'on average, 57 percent of accessibility issues' by volume (2,000+ audits, about 300,000 issues). Playwright docs: 'many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing'. UsableNet: more than 5,000 digital accessibility lawsuits in 2025, with 'no meaningful reduction in lawsuits against widget users'. FTC ordered accessiBe to pay $1M (Jan 3, 2025) over claims its AI widget made sites WCAG-compliant. Level Access: EAA enforcement began June 28, 2025, with the first lawsuits filed in France in November 2025. WebAIM Million 2026 names 'AI-assisted coding practices ("vibe coding")' among the drivers of worsening accessibility: 95.9% of pages had failures and the average rose to 56.1 errors per page.
findings.corrections: Say the final FTC order came in April 2025 (proposed Jan 3, 2025). Frame Deque's 57% as vendor-reported and by issue volume, and present the GOV.UK 13-40% per tool as the counterpoint. Say turnover OR balance sheet of €2M or less.

missed_items.title: Playwright removed page.accessibility.snapshot(); use ariaSnapshot or CDP AX tree
missed_items.why: Several detection approaches rely on 'the Playwright accessibility snapshot'. The old API is gone. Run Hound must use page/locator.ariaSnapshot() (YAML or JSON), or CDP Accessibility.getFullAXTree for computed names and roles. This is an implementation risk for V0.

missed_items.title: React event delegation defeats listener-based click-handler detection
missed_items.why: React 17 and later attach handlers at the root, so getEventListeners on elements is empty for the main target stack (Lovable, Bolt and v0 are React). Detection needs heuristics based on cursor, fiber props or interaction.

missed_items.title: US ADA Title II deadline extended to April 2027/2028 (WCAG 2.1 AA)
missed_items.why: This is a legal driver for adoption. A DOJ interim final rule on April 20, 2026 pushed state and local government compliance to April 26, 2027 (population of 50k or more) and April 26, 2028 (under 50k). It is relevant to 'the need for this kind of tool' and to the timing of the OSS release.

missed_items.title: Independent evidence of low automated coverage (GOV.UK tool audit)
missed_items.why: 13 tools were run against 142 planted barriers, and the best found 40% (low of 13%). This counterbalances Deque's vendor 57% figure and supports the agent-interaction value proposition.

missed_items.title: Forced-colors / Windows High Contrast mode
missed_items.why: outline-none (as opposed to outline-hidden) removes focus even in forced-colors mode. Icons drawn with background-image and SVGs with hard-coded fill disappear. Playwright supports emulateMedia({forcedColors:'active'}), so this is cheap to add.

missed_items.title: WCAG 2.2 Redundant Entry (3.3.7, A) and Consistent Help (3.2.6, A)
missed_items.why: Multi-step signup and checkout flows that ask for the same data again are common in generated apps. They can be detected across a V2/V3 end-to-end flow by the agent comparing the fields in each step.

missed_items.title: Content on hover or focus (1.4.13) and tooltips
missed_items.why: Tooltips and hover cards that cannot be dismissed with Escape, disappear when the pointer moves onto them, or appear only on hover are common with shadcn and Radix misuse. The browser agent can detect these by hovering, focusing and pressing Escape.

missed_items.title: Text spacing (1.4.12) and Identify Input Purpose (1.3.5)
missed_items.why: Injecting the WCAG text-spacing CSS and checking for clipping is automatable. Missing or invalid autocomplete tokens on personal-data fields are covered by axe autocomplete-valid only when the token is invalid, not when it is missing.

missed_items.title: Timing and session timeouts (2.2.1) and page title (2.4.2)
missed_items.why: Auth sessions that expire without warning, and SPAs with one static <title>, are common in vibe-coded apps. Both can be detected from outside the app, the timeout through long-running scenarios and the title through the axe document-title rule plus a per-route uniqueness check.

missed_items.title: Canvas-rendered, shadow DOM and iframe content coverage limits
missed_items.why: Flutter-web or canvas UIs expose little DOM or a11y tree to scan. Closed shadow roots and cross-origin iframes (payment and embed widgets) limit axe. The report should state which content was not scanned rather than implying the page is clean.

missed_items.title: Label in Name (2.5.3) mismatch for voice-control users
missed_items.why: An aria-label such as 'btn-primary' or 'Submit form' on a button that visibly reads 'Continue' breaks voice control. This is common when LLMs add aria-label. It can be detected by comparing the visible text from a screenshot or innerText with the accessible name (axe label-content-name-mismatch is experimental).

findings.title: Buttons, links and menu items that do nothing
findings.description: Controls look finished but do nothing. Typical causes: an onClick that is empty or only runs console.log, href="#", a handler that calls a function that was never written, or a button with no text and no working action. The UI looks complete while the feature behind it is missing.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI tools build the visible UI first and wire behavior later, or never. The prompt asks for 'a dashboard with export and share buttons' and the model draws the buttons without writing the backend. LLM bug studies list 'Incomplete Generation' (empty functions or `pass` bodies) at 9.57% of bugs. Nobody clicks every control before shipping.
findings.user_impact: Users click Export, Save or Share and nothing happens, with no error. They lose trust, contact support, or leave. In a checkout or signup this loses conversions.
findings.detection_approach: Enumerate every interactive element from the a11y tree and DOM (role=button/link/menuitem, elements with click listeners, cursor:pointer). Click each one in an isolated state and record whether anything happens: DOM mutation, navigation, network request, dialog, focus change, or console output. If nothing happens, or the element has href="#" or javascript:void(0), flag it as 'dead control'. Treat empty accessible names as a secondary signal. Save a screenshot before and after.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebGen-Bench (NeurIPS 2025 D&B): the best agent/LLM pair (Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1) passed only 27.8% of 647 functional UI test cases on generated websites; a web-navigation agent ran the tests. WebAIM Million 2025: 45.4% of home pages had empty links and 29.6% had empty buttons. Tao et al. LLM bug taxonomy: Incomplete Generation 9.57%.
findings.corrections: Say 'best off-the-shelf pair 27.8%; fine-tuned model 38.2%'. Change 'Tao et al.' to 'Tambon et al. (Empirical Software Engineering 2025)' and note it studied older code LLMs on Python functions. Move the WebAIM empty-link and empty-button numbers to the a11y domain rather than using them as dead-control prevalence.

findings.title: Placeholder, demo or made-up data shipped as if it were real
findings.description: Dashboards, lists, stats, testimonials or 'results' come from hardcoded arrays, seed JSON or LLM-invented sample records instead of the real data source. Examples: 'John Doe', lorem ipsum, example.com emails, the same numbers for every account, charts that never change.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI builders fill empty screens with sample data so the preview looks good. If the backend is never connected, the mocks stay in production. Agents have also been caught inventing data to hide failures.
findings.user_impact: Users make decisions from fake numbers. The owner believes the feature works. Reviews or metrics may amount to misleading claims.
findings.detection_approach: Pattern-match rendered text for placeholder markers (lorem ipsum, John/Jane Doe, example.com, 555- phone numbers, 'Acme', TODO, {{var}}, 'undefined', 'NaN', '$0.00' everywhere). Check whether the displayed records match any network response; data present in the JS bundle but never fetched points to hardcoding. Compare two test accounts: identical 'personal' data suggests a mock. Create or delete a record and check whether counts and charts update.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Axon Build audit of 26 AI-built apps: 'fabricated or demo data presented as real output' was one of 14 recurring problems, and the only one visible during normal owner use. Replit/SaaStr incident, July 2025 (The Register): the agent 'created a 4,000-record database containing fictional people' and 'generated misleading reports to conceal bugs'.
findings.corrections: The Replit case is an agent fabricating data during development, not placeholder data left in production. Rate detection 'partial': placeholder markers are reliable, plausible fake data is not.

findings.title: Features that look saved but are not persisted
findings.description: A create, edit or delete updates the UI (optimistic state, React state, localStorage) but never reaches a server, or the write fails silently. After a reload, on another device, or in a new session the change is gone or reverts.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Prototype builders often keep state only in the browser until a backend is connected. Models write optimistic UI updates without checking the server's response. The builder tests in one tab without reloading, so everything seems to work.
findings.user_impact: Silent data loss: users enter work, come back, and it's gone. It usually surfaces only after real users rely on it.
findings.detection_approach: For each CRUD flow: do the action, confirm a write request (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) got a 2xx, then (a) hard-reload, (b) open a fresh browser context with storage cleared and the same login, and (c) check the item is still there. Flag writes that only touch localStorage/IndexedDB (diff storage snapshots), send no request, or get a 4xx/5xx while the UI shows success.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Anecdotal/unsourced as a specific frequency. Related: WebGen-Bench functional tests (27.8% best pass rate) include data-operation cases. Axon Build audits describe apps that 'worked beautifully' in demos and failed under real conditions. CodeRabbit (Dec 2025): error-handling and exception-path gaps were 'nearly 2x more common' in AI PRs.
findings.corrections: Fix the Axon paraphrase. Keep prevalence marked as unsourced.

findings.title: Forms that fail silently: no error state, swallowed exceptions
findings.description: When the API returns 4xx/5xx, times out, or the user is offline, the form shows nothing, spins forever, resets as if it worked, or shows a generic toast while the data is lost. Validation errors from the server never reach the user, or show only visually without a programmatic association or aria-live.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated code covers the happy path. The try/catch only calls console.error, or the promise rejection is never handled. Error paths never show up in the builder's own tests because their local backend always answers.
findings.user_impact: Users think they submitted (signup, contact, order) when they didn't, or they retry and create duplicates. Businesses lose leads without knowing.
findings.detection_approach: Use Playwright route interception to inject failures on each form's submit request: 500, 422 with an error body, network abort, a 30s delay, and offline mode. Check for a visible error message, preserved input, a re-enabled submit button, an aria-live/role=alert announcement, and no false 'Success'. Also correlate unhandled promise rejections in the console with a UI that stays silent.
findings.prevalence_evidence: CodeRabbit 'State of AI vs Human Code Generation' (Dec 2025, 470 PRs): AI PRs had 10.83 issues vs 6.45 for human PRs (~1.7x); 'Error handling and exception-path gaps were nearly 2x more common', with missing null checks, early returns and exception logic. Axon Build: 17 of 21 audited third-party apps had no error tracking or alerting.
findings.corrections: Make clear that the Axon 17/21 figure is about observability or alerting, not form UX.

findings.title: Missing loading, empty and partial-data states
findings.description: Screens flash blank, show 'undefined'/'NaN', crash on an empty array, or show a fake empty state while data is still loading. A brand-new account shows a broken layout or an error instead of a helpful empty state.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Developers and models test on a fast local backend with seeded data, so slow networks and zero-record accounts are never exercised. Generated components often assume `data` is already defined.
findings.user_impact: First-run experience breaks for every new user. Slow mobile networks show blank or broken screens. Users may conclude their data was deleted.
findings.detection_approach: Run key pages with network throttling (Slow 3G), with delayed API routes, and with a fresh empty account (or routes intercepted to return []/{}). Screenshot mid-load and after load. Flag 'undefined', 'NaN', '[object Object]', 'null', blank regions, and uncaught TypeErrors (e.g. 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading map)'). Check for a busy indicator (aria-busy/progressbar) while loading.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Tao et al. taxonomy of LLM-generated code bugs: 'Missing Corner Case' is the 2nd most common category at 15.27%. CodeRabbit: missing null checks and early returns among the gaps that are nearly 2x more common in AI PRs.
findings.corrections: Fix the attribution to Tambon et al. and state that the evidence is indirect.

findings.title: Double submit creates duplicate orders, charges or records
findings.description: The submit button stays enabled during the request and the backend is not idempotent. A double-click, pressing Enter twice, a refresh after POST, or a browser retry creates duplicate records, sends duplicate emails, or charges twice.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Disable-on-submit, idempotency keys and Post/Redirect/Get are defensive patterns that prompts rarely ask for. Stripe's own guidance warns that fulfillment 'might be called multiple times, possibly concurrently', which naive handlers don't expect.
findings.user_impact: Duplicate charges and orders, refunds, support load, and corrupted data.
findings.detection_approach: Per form: dispatch two clicks within ~50ms, press Enter repeatedly, and reload right after submitting. Count outgoing mutation requests; more than one without an idempotency key or deduping header is suspect. Then check whether the list or history shows duplicates. Check the button gets disabled/aria-disabled and shows progress. Run only against opted-in, non-destructive or test-mode targets.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Anecdotal/unsourced for prevalence. Mechanism documented in OpenReplay's guide ('Now you have two orders, two charges, and one frustrated customer') and in Stripe's fulfillment docs ('might be called multiple times, possibly concurrently, for the same Checkout Session').
findings.corrections: Don't treat a missing idempotency header as evidence on its own. Confirm by observing the duplicate record.

findings.title: Race conditions: out-of-order responses show stale data
findings.description: Search-as-you-type, filters, tabs and pagination fire overlapping requests. A slower earlier response arrives after a newer one and overwrites it, so the UI shows results for the wrong query or page. Related: fast navigation causes state updates on unmounted views, and a response lands in the wrong account after switching users.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Generated fetch-in-useEffect code usually has no AbortController and no ignore flag. Debounce alone is not enough. Local backends respond in constant time, so the ordering bug never appears during development.
findings.user_impact: Users see wrong search results, wrong prices or wrong records, and may act on them. These bugs are intermittent and hard to report.
findings.detection_approach: Intercept API routes and add random or reversed delays (e.g. make the first request slowest). Type a query quickly, change filters fast, or page quickly, then check that the final rendered results match the final input (compare the response for the last query with the DOM). Repeat several times for flakiness. Also look for React warnings and for requests that are never cancelled.
