findings.prevalence_evidence: CodeRabbit (Dec 2025): 'Concurrency and dependency correctness saw ~2x increases' in AI-authored PRs. GreatFrontEnd documents the pattern: 'the response for the term toma can arrive later than the response for the term tomato'.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Payment 'success' granted from the redirect page, not a verified webhook
findings.description: The app grants paid access or marks an order paid because the browser landed on /success (often with a session_id it never checks against the provider). Real payments whose redirect never loads go unfulfilled. Anyone who visits the success URL directly may get paid features for free.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: The success-page approach is the simplest to write and it looks right in the builder's test. Webhooks need a server endpoint, signature verification and idempotency, which AI builders often skip or stub.
findings.user_impact: Revenue loss (free upgrades), customers charged but not provisioned, and duplicate provisioning.
findings.detection_approach: Test mode only, with owner opt-in. (1) Find the success/return URL in the checkout flow or JS bundle. (2) In a fresh free account, open it directly with no session_id, a fake one, and a reused one. Flag any plan or entitlement change in the UI or in /me-type API responses. (3) Watch whether the entitlement change follows only the client redirect with no server confirmation. Whether a webhook exists can't be confirmed from outside, which makes this partial.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Anecdotal/unsourced for frequency in vibe-coded apps. Stripe docs state it outright: 'You can't rely on triggering fulfilment only from your checkout landing page, because it's not guaranteed customers visit that page', and 'Webhooks are required for fulfilment'.
findings.corrections: Reword: landing-page fulfillment is recommended alongside webhooks. The bug is unverified client-side grant plus a missing webhook.

findings.title: OAuth/magic-link redirects go to localhost or the wrong domain in production
findings.description: After Google/GitHub login or a magic link, users land on http://localhost:3000, a preview domain, or a blank page. The cause is an unchanged Site URL or a redirect allow-list that doesn't match production, and the auth provider falls back silently.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Supabase-style auth defaults the Site URL to localhost and, per practitioner reports, silently falls back to it when a redirectTo isn't allow-listed. AI builders configure auth in dev and nobody re-checks after deploy or a domain change.
findings.user_impact: Nobody can log in on the production site, and there's no error message.
findings.detection_approach: Start each social or magic-link login and follow the redirect chain. Inspect redirect_to/redirect_uri query params and Location headers for localhost, 127.0.0.1, preview hosts, or hosts that don't match the app origin. Flag a final landing on an unreachable host or with error fragments (#error=...). Also grep the JS bundles for hardcoded localhost auth callback URLs. Stop before entering third-party credentials unless a test account is provided.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Supabase docs: Site URL 'defines the default redirect URL when no redirectTo is specified'; change it 'from http://localhost:3000 to your production URL'. DEV article: Supabase 'falls back to the Site URL... silently, with no error page and no console warning'. GitHub issue supabase#12941 reports signInWithOAuth always redirecting to localhost:3000 in production.
findings.corrections: Rate 'partial' unless a test identity or inbox is provided. Credit the fallback claim to the DEV article and the GitHub reports, not the Supabase docs.

findings.title: Password reset, email verification and magic links broken in production
findings.description: Emails never arrive (the default dev SMTP only sends to team members, rate limits are hit), the link points to the API or a localhost URL, the token is consumed or lost during a redirect ('token is missing'), or the reset page logs the user in without letting them set a password.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: These flows depend on out-of-band infrastructure (SMTP, email templates, redirect allow-lists) that AI builders don't configure. The developer tests with their own team email address, which the default SMTP allows, so the flow looks like it works.
findings.user_impact: New users can't verify accounts and existing users are locked out. Signups quietly drop off and support tickets grow.
findings.detection_approach: Trigger signup, reset and magic-link flows and watch the network for 429 or 'Email address not authorized' errors, plus UI that says 'check your email' even when the request failed. With an owner-supplied test inbox (or a Mailpit/IMAP hook), open the received link, then check the redirect host, that the reset form renders, that the new password works, and that the link can't be reused. Without an inbox, only the request side can be checked, which makes this partial.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Supabase SMTP docs: the default server sends 'only to pre-authorized addresses', is capped at '2 messages per hour', and has 'no SLA'. Latenode community thread on Supabase+Lovable reset failures cites 'token is missing' errors and redirect/callback mismatches. The frequency itself is anecdotal.
findings.corrections: Quote the actual error: 'Verify requires a token or a token hash'.

findings.title: Refresh, deep links and the Back button break on SPA routes
findings.description: Client-side routes work when clicked but 404 on reload or when opened directly or shared, because the host has no rewrite to index.html. Related: Back/Forward loses filters, form input, scroll position or the modal state. URLs don't reflect state, so links can't be shared.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: The dev server rewrites routes automatically, but static hosts need an explicit rule (e.g. Netlify `/* /index.html 200`). Beginners don't know this, and AI builders' previews hide it.
findings.user_impact: Shared or bookmarked links land on 404s, a refresh 'breaks the app', and users lose work when they press Back.
findings.detection_approach: For every route the crawler reaches by clicking: open it directly in a new context and hard-reload it. Check the HTTP status (a 404 document or the host's error page is a failure) and that the content matches the clicked render. Test Back/Forward after filtering, paginating and filling forms, and check URL and state consistency. Report any route that fails to render its own content on refresh.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Netlify support guide: direct links and refreshes on routes other than '/' in SPAs 404 without the `/* /index.html 200` rewrite. It is one of Netlify's canonical support guides. Frequency is otherwise anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Dead links, missing assets and broken internal navigation
findings.description: Links and images point to pages that don't exist or were renamed, missing assets, or template leftovers (/about, /blog, /privacy placeholders, # anchors with no target). Footers and nav from AI templates often link to pages that were never built.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI templates generate full nav and footer link sets ('Careers', 'Blog', 'Terms') for pages nobody creates. Renames during AI edits leave old links behind.
findings.user_impact: 404s erode credibility. Missing Privacy/Terms pages can create compliance problems. Broken images degrade the page.
findings.detection_approach: Crawl same-origin pages, collect every href/src/srcset/CSS url, and HEAD/GET them. Flag 4xx/5xx, soft-404s (200 with 'not found' content), anchors whose #id doesn't exist, and images that fail (naturalWidth == 0). Check external links politely (no deep crawling of third-party sites).
findings.prevalence_evidence: Pew Research (May 2024): '23% of news webpages contain at least one broken link, as do 21% of webpages from government sites'; 'a quarter of all webpages that existed at one point between 2013 and 2023 are no longer accessible'. This is general web data, not specific to vibe-coded apps.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: SSR hydration mismatches (Next.js/React)
findings.description:
Server-rendered HTML differs from the first client render, causing console errors, content that flickers or re-renders, and sometimes event handlers that don't attach. Common causes: Date() or locale formatting in render, window/localStorage checks, invalid nesting (
in

, in ,
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: LLMs mix browser-only APIs and time-dependent values into server components and produce invalid HTML nesting (e.g. a card wrapped in a link that contains buttons). Developers ignore the red console overlay or paper over it with suppressHydrationWarning.
findings.user_impact: Flicker, layout shift, wrong content (server vs client time), and in the worst case parts of the page that don't respond until a re-render. Crawlers and screen readers can see different content from sighted users.
findings.detection_approach: Capture console errors and warnings on first load for messages like 'Hydration failed', 'did not match', 'Text content does not match server-rendered HTML', and minified React errors #418/#423/#425. Compare the raw server HTML (response body) with the post-hydration DOM text. Validate nesting of interactive content in the DOM. Re-run in a different timezone/locale to trigger date-based mismatches.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Next.js official docs list the common causes: invalid nesting, `typeof window` checks, browser-only APIs, 'time-dependent APIs such as the Date() constructor', and browser extensions. Frequency is anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: Rate 'partial' in production builds. Rely on comparing raw HTML with the hydrated DOM, not only on console text.

findings.title: Timezone and locale bugs (off-by-one dates, wrong formats)
findings.description: Dates shift by a day depending on the user's timezone (e.g. a 'YYYY-MM-DD' birthday or due date shown as the previous day), bookings fall in the wrong slot, 'today' filters are wrong near midnight, and currency or number formats break for non-US locales. A value saved via a date input changes after reload.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: JavaScript Date parses date-only strings as UTC but date-time strings as local time, and LLMs reproduce these patterns. Developers test only in their own timezone and locale.
findings.user_impact: Wrong appointments, deadlines and invoices. Every user outside the developer's timezone is affected.
findings.detection_approach: Run the same scenarios in multiple Playwright contexts with different timezoneId (e.g. America/Los_Angeles, Pacific/Kiritimati, Asia/Kolkata with its half-hour offset) and locale (en-US, de-DE, ja-JP), plus a mocked clock near midnight or a DST boundary. Enter a date, save, reload, and compare the displayed value across contexts. Flag differences and off-by-one results. Also check number and currency parsing with comma decimals.
findings.prevalence_evidence: MDN: 'date-only forms are interpreted as a UTC time and date-time forms are interpreted as a local time... due to a historical spec error'. Next.js docs list Date() in render as a hydration cause. Frequency is anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Production config missing: undefined env vars, localhost API URLs, dev-only settings
findings.description: The deployed app calls http://localhost:3001/api, 'undefined/api/...', or a preview backend because build-time env vars were missing or lacked the right prefix (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_). Features that worked in the builder fail in production. Secret keys get prefixed to 'make it work' and end up exposed in the bundle.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Vite and Next statically inline env vars at build time. A missing or unprefixed variable becomes undefined without an obvious error. Beginners respond by adding the public prefix to secrets.
findings.user_impact: Whole features are dead in production (CORS/connection errors), or secrets leak.
findings.detection_approach: Monitor all network requests for hosts equal to localhost, 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0, literal 'undefined'/'null' in URLs, preview/staging hosts, or mixed content. Scan the JS bundles for such base URLs and for key patterns (sk_live, service_role and similar). Correlate with console errors such as ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED and CORS failures.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Vite docs: VITE_ variables are 'statically replaced at build time' and 'VITE_* variables should not contain sensitive information'. Escape.tech black-box scan of 5,600 vibe-coded apps (Lovable, Base44, Create.xyz, Bolt.new) found 400+ exposed secrets through frontend bundle analysis.
findings.corrections: Say 'several methods including JS bundle analysis'. The localhost and undefined-URL failure has no prevalence evidence.

findings.title: Broken mobile/responsive layouts and zoom blocking
findings.description: Horizontal scroll at phone widths, overlapping or cut-off content, nav menus that don't open or can't be reached, modals taller than the viewport with no scroll, fixed elements covering CTAs, tiny tap targets, and pinch-zoom disabled via the viewport meta tag.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI builders preview and iterate on desktop canvases. Generated fixed widths (w-[1200px]), absolutely positioned elements and hover-only menus break on touch. Templates often ship with user-scalable=no.
findings.user_impact: Most consumer traffic is mobile, so core flows (signup, checkout) can become unusable. Low-vision users can't zoom (a WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10 failure).
findings.detection_approach: Re-run the golden-path scenarios in device emulation (320, 375 and 414 px widths, touch enabled, portrait and landscape). Check document.scrollWidth > clientWidth, elements outside the viewport, overlapping bounding boxes of interactive elements, targets smaller than 24x24 CSS px, and that the menu opens by tap. Inspect the viewport meta for user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1. Compare screenshots with vision to catch clipped text.
findings.prevalence_evidence: HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2024 (Accessibility chapter): '16% of mobile sites disable scaling' via user-scalable=no, '20% set a maximum-scale of 1', 23% use either. There is no sourced figure for responsive-layout breakage specific to vibe-coded apps (anecdotal).
findings.corrections: Cite WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 for the 24px target threshold.

findings.title: Regressions when an AI edit fixes one thing and breaks another (the 'doom loop')
findings.description: A prompt to fix bug A silently breaks feature B, or reintroduces an earlier bug, because the agent edits without a dependency map, rewrites whole files, or duplicates logic, so one copy gets fixed and the other doesn't. Without regression tests nobody notices until users do.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Context limits, non-deterministic generation, copy-paste over refactoring, and patches aimed at the visible symptom. Vibe coders have no test suite and judge by what they see in one preview. Most audited AI-built apps had no working automated tests.
findings.user_impact: Features that worked last week break without anyone noticing, and trust in the product erodes.
findings.detection_approach: Run Hound's exported Playwright specs become a regression baseline. Re-run the approved scenario suite after each change (CLI/CI hook), diff results, screenshots (visual diff), a11y-tree snapshots and network contracts (request/response shapes) against the last green run, and flag newly failing golden paths. It's partial because it only catches regressions in flows that were already captured.
findings.prevalence_evidence: GitClear (via DevClass, Feb 2025; 211M changed lines): code blocks with 5+ duplicated lines rose 8x in 2024, moved (refactored) lines fell 39.9%. SWE-Bench+ (arXiv 2410.06992): '31.08% of the passed patches are suspicious patches due to weak test cases'. Axon Build: 23 of 26 audited AI-built apps had zero working automated tests.
findings.corrections: Say 'at least 23 of 26'.

findings.title: Code calls functions, endpoints or fields that don't exist, causing runtime errors
findings.description: Generated code references functions, object properties, SDK methods or API routes that don't exist ('x is not a function', 404 on /api/v1/whatever, reading a field the backend never returns). Often it breaks only on the branch that's rarely exercised.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: LLMs 'hallucinate objects' that fit the prompt's vocabulary and mix up SDK versions. Beginners can't tell a plausible API from a real one, and the broken branch isn't exercised in the demo.
findings.user_impact: Features crash partway through, often only on secondary paths (edit, delete, export, settings).
findings.detection_approach: During exploration, capture uncaught exceptions and console errors (TypeError: ... is not a function / undefined), failed chunk loads, and API calls that return 404/405 for app-own routes. Map each error to the step and element that triggered it, and include the stack from source maps if present. Explore beyond the golden path (edit, delete, secondary tabs) to reach rarely used branches.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Tao et al. (Empirical Software Engineering 2025, arXiv 2403.08937; 333 bugs): Hallucinated Object 9.57%, Wrong Attribute 8.55%, Misinterpretation 20.77% (most common).
findings.corrections: Change the attribution to Tambon et al. and note the older models and Python scope.

findings.title: Search, filter, sort and pagination that only work on small sample data or the happy path
findings.description: Search is case-sensitive or exact-match, breaks on special characters or unicode, and shows no 'no results' state. Pagination drops or duplicates items at page boundaries, the 'next' button stays active on the last page, or everything is loaded client-side and fails beyond a few hundred records. Sorting is lexicographic ('10' before '9'). Inputs have no length limits.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Built and demoed against 5-10 seed records. Models skip corner cases and prefer simple, I/O-heavy approaches (fetch all, filter in the browser).
findings.user_impact: Real users can't find their data, lists are wrong, and pages slow down or freeze as data grows.
findings.detection_approach: Fuzz search and filter inputs (mixed case, accents/emoji, quotes, %, _, very long strings, leading/trailing spaces, empty), assert that results are consistent and a proper empty state appears. Walk pagination to the end, checking for duplicate or missing IDs across pages and the disabled state of 'next'. Check sort order on numeric and date columns. Watch whether a list request returns the entire dataset (large payloads with no page params). It's partial because proving scale behavior needs seeded volume (optional owner-approved seeding or intercepted large mock responses).
findings.prevalence_evidence: Tao et al.: 'Missing Corner Case' is 15.27% of LLM-generated code bugs (code 'fails on one or a few exceptional test inputs'). CodeRabbit (Dec 2025): 'Excessive I/O operations were ~8x more common in AI-authored PRs'.
findings.corrections: Fix the attribution.

findings.title: 'Looks done' and 'AI says done': no one independently verifies features (the need for this tool)
findings.description: This is a cross-cutting pattern: builders accept the AI's claim, or a quick visual preview, as proof that a feature works. Agents have reported passing tests that didn't pass, and developers consistently overrate how much AI helped. The result is apps that pass the demo and fail real use.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Non-technical builders can't read the code. Output that is 'almost right' passes a casual look. There are no tests, and agent-written tests can be weak or fabricated.
findings.user_impact: Users hit the bugs first, and owners find out through churn, refunds or incidents.
findings.detection_approach: This is Run Hound's core value proposition: an independent black-box verifier. Generate golden-path and danger-path scenarios from the a11y tree, DOM and vision, execute them, verify outcomes against network and persisted state (not just the UI), and export repeatable Playwright specs so 'done' is backed by evidence.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey (AI section): 66% cite 'AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite' as their top frustration, 45% say debugging AI code takes longer, only 3.1% 'highly trust' AI output accuracy. METR RCT (July 2025, 16 experienced OSS devs, 246 issues): AI use made tasks take 19% longer, yet developers believed it sped them up by 20%. Replit/SaaStr (The Register, July 2025): the agent 'lied about unit test outcomes'. WebGen-Bench: best pass rate 27.8%.
findings.corrections: Qualify WebGen-Bench as best off-the-shelf. The Replit test claim is a first-person anecdote.

missed_items.title: Stale chunk loads after redeploy (ChunkLoadError or 'Failed to fetch dynamically imported module')
missed_items.why: Frequent on Vite/Next apps that redeploy often, as vibe-coded apps do. Open tabs break on navigation. Detectable from the browser: keep a context open across a deploy, or intercept chunk requests with a 404, and watch for the vite:preloadError event or a console error.

missed_items.title: Broken authorization/data isolation that looks like a feature bug (missing Supabase RLS, one user sees another's data)
missed_items.why: The most damaging vibe-coding failure on record. Overlaps with the security domain but shows up as 'wrong data in my list'. Detectable with two test accounts (cross-account IDOR checks). CVE-2025-48757: 170 of 1,645 Lovable apps (10.3%) exposed.

missed_items.title: Session expiry and token refresh failures
missed_items.why: Users get logged out mid-task, or get stuck in a half-authenticated state after the JWT expires, and forms fail silently with 401s. Detectable by expiring or deleting tokens, mocking the clock, or intercepting 401s.

missed_items.title: Cross-browser failures (Safari/WebKit, Firefox)
missed_items.why: Builders preview in Chromium only. Date inputs, clipboard APIs and newer JS or CSS features break on iOS Safari. Playwright ships WebKit and Firefox, so this is cheap to add to the danger path.

missed_items.title: File upload flows (storage bucket policies, size and type limits, public buckets)
missed_items.why: Common feature in AI-built apps. Failures include silent 403s from storage policies, missing error states on oversized files, and uploads served from public buckets. Detectable with test files and by inspecting network traffic.

missed_items.title: Performance and Core Web Vitals regressions (huge bundles, fetch-everything lists)
missed_items.why: Many sites still fail Core Web Vitals. AI code tends toward heavy I/O (CodeRabbit ~8x). Measurable from the browser with the Performance API, LCP/INP/CLS and payload sizes.

findings.title: Backend database/storage left open (Supabase RLS off, Firebase test-mode rules)
findings.description: AI-generated apps talk to Supabase or Firebase directly from the browser. If row-level security or security rules are missing or permissive, any visitor can read or write other users' rows or files.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Supabase tables start without RLS enabled, and Firebase test mode is wide open; AI scaffolding and novices ship these defaults because the app 'works'.
findings.user_impact: Mass exposure of user records, IDs, messages, payment data; possible data tampering or deletion.
findings.detection_approach: On owner-verified targets only: observe which backend endpoints the app itself calls, then as a second seeded test account check whether data belonging to the first account is returned. Report in plain language: 'Another logged-in user could see data that belongs to someone else.' Do not enumerate beyond the owner's own seeded test data.
findings.prevalence_evidence: CVE-2025-48757: 170 of 1,645 scanned Lovable apps exposed, 303 vulnerable endpoints (Superblocks write-up). Tea app: 72,000 images incl. ~13,000 selfies/IDs exposed via unsecured Firebase storage (Engadget, Jul 2025). Escape.tech: 2,038 critical vulns, 400+ secrets, 175 PII exposures across vibe-coded apps.
findings.corrections: Say '170 of 1,645 Lovable showcase apps (~10%), 303 endpoints (Matt Palmer, CVE-2025-48757)', not 'Superblocks'. Escape scanned about 1.4K apps. The 13,000 selfies/IDs figure should cite Tea's statement or 404 Media, not Engadget.

findings.title: Access control enforced only in the browser
findings.description: Admin pages, paid features or 'inactive' states are hidden with frontend route guards or flags, while the server API does not re-check who the user is.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI tools generate UI-level guards that look like security; novices assume a hidden button means a blocked action.
findings.user_impact: Users can reach features or data they should not; account takeover or privilege escalation.
findings.detection_approach: Using the owner's test accounts, compare what a low-privilege account's API calls return versus what the UI shows; flag pages that render protected content after a hard reload or direct URL visit while logged out. Explain: 'Your app hides this page, but the server still hands out the data.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Synack documents three real pentest cases of client-side auth bypass; Wiz found Base44 platform flaw letting unauthenticated users register on private apps using a public app_id (Jul 2025).
findings.corrections: Replace or relabel the Base44 example as a 'platform auth flaw'. Better evidence is the Synack cases plus OWASP A01 Broken Access Control, which is the #1 category.

findings.title: Runaway LLM/cloud API bills (denial of wallet)
findings.description: AI features call paid model APIs with no per-user quota, rate limit or input size cap; unrestricted keys for paid Google APIs are similar.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders focus on the demo working; rate limiting and billing alerts are invisible until the invoice arrives.
findings.user_impact: Surprise bills in the thousands; service suspension.
findings.detection_approach: Note when the browser calls model providers directly instead of the app's own backend; check whether the app's AI endpoint shows any rate-limit response (429) under a small, owner-approved burst. Explain: 'Nothing stops one visitor from running up your AI bill. Add limits and a spending cap.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: OWASP LLM10:2025 defines Unbounded Consumption incl. Denial of Wallet. Google: 'You are financially responsible for charges caused by abuse of unrestricted API keys.' RedHunt Labs found AI-platform credentials among ~25,000 secrets leaked from ~26,000 of ~130,000 vibe-coded sites (Sep 2025).
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Misunderstanding which environment variables become public
findings.description: Framework prefixes (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_) inline values into client code at build time; builders believe anything in .env is private.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: '.env' sounds secret; AI assistants add the prefix to make an error go away.
findings.user_impact: Configuration intended to be private ends up visible to every visitor.
findings.detection_approach: Report which configuration values appear in shipped client code and explain in plain language that anything in the browser is public, with a pointer to move sensitive calls server-side.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Vite docs: 'VITE_* variables should not contain sensitive information such as API keys. The values of these variables are bundled into your source code at build time.' Intruder attributes many bundle exposures to build-time env injection mistakes (Dec 2025).
findings.corrections: Soften the Intruder attribution to 'Intruder documents a case where a build script injected all of process.env into the bundle; it found 42,000+ tokens across 5M apps'.

findings.title: Dev vs prod confusion: localhost URLs, test-mode keys, mixed content, shared DB
findings.description: Production builds still point at localhost APIs, use test/sandbox payment keys, load http:// resources, or dev and prod share one database.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI generators default to localhost:3000/5173; non-technical builders have no concept of separate environments.
findings.user_impact: Forms hang silently, payments never charge, or a dev action wipes production data.
findings.detection_approach: Flag network requests to localhost/127.0.0.1/private IPs, http:// requests blocked as mixed content, and test-mode indicators in payment widgets. Explain: 'Your live site is trying to talk to your own laptop.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Replit agent deleted SaaStr production DB (Jul 2025); Replit then added automatic dev/prod DB separation (The Register). MDN: fetch/XHR/scripts over http on https pages are blocked.
findings.corrections: Cite theregister.com/2025/07/22/replit_saastr_response/ or x.com/amasad/status/1946986468586721478 for the separation fix. A shared DB cannot be observed from the browser.

findings.title: No database backups or recovery plan
findings.description: Free-tier backends often have no automatic backups; builders don't know until data is lost.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Backups are an ops concern invisible in the app; AI agents with DB access can destroy data.
findings.user_impact: Permanent loss of all user data.
findings.detection_approach: Not observable from the browser. Include in a pre-launch checklist section: 'We can't see this — confirm you have automatic backups and have tested a restore.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Supabase docs: free plan projects should 'regularly export their data using the Supabase CLI db dump command and maintain off-site backups'; 'Database backups are not available for download for Free Plan projects.' Replit/SaaStr incident.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Tracking cookies/pixels fire before or despite cookie consent
findings.description: Analytics and ad pixels load on first page view, or keep firing after the user clicks Reject.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders paste a banner and assume it blocks scripts; AI adds analytics snippets in the head.
findings.user_impact: GDPR/ePrivacy exposure and fines; loss of user trust.
findings.detection_approach: Fresh context: record cookies and third-party requests before any interaction, after Reject, and after Accept. Flag known tracker domains firing pre-consent or post-reject. Explain: 'Your site tracks visitors before they agree.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Compilation of 29 studies cites 43.1% of sites setting tracking cookies without valid consent (ScienceDirect 2025) and 24% continuing after Reject (arXiv 2026).
findings.corrections: Cite the primary studies rather than the vendor roundup.

findings.title: Personal data leaking to analytics and ad pixels
findings.description: Emails, names, search terms or health/purchase info flow to third parties via URLs (GET forms), page titles, or pixel auto-capture of form fields.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: GET forms and auto-event tracking are defaults; builders don't inspect what pixels send.
findings.user_impact: Privacy violations, regulator action, analytics account termination.
findings.detection_approach: Submit forms with unique canary values; search all third-party request URLs and payloads for them. Explain: 'The email a user typed was sent to Google/Meta.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: FTC: pixels can send 'information users have typed within a form'; GoodRx paid $1.5M penalty. Google Analytics: 'Both the URL path and parameters must be free of PII.'
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: No privacy policy, account deletion, or data-request path
findings.description: Apps collect accounts but offer no privacy policy link, no delete-account flow, and no contact for data requests.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI builds the happy path; legal obligations aren't in the prompt.
findings.user_impact: Inability to meet GDPR/UK GDPR erasure duties (one month) and app-store/legal requirements.
findings.detection_approach: Check for a reachable privacy policy link on signup/footer, and a delete-account option in settings; test deletion with a seeded account then attempt to log in. Explain what the law expects in plain words.
findings.prevalence_evidence: ICO: respond to erasure 'without undue delay and at the latest within one month'; requests may be verbal. Prevalence of missing flows: anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Site invisible to search and social: SPA rendering, soft 404s, leftover noindex, no OG tags
findings.description: Client-rendered SPAs return empty HTML, 200 for missing pages, hash routes, staging robots.txt Disallow or noindex shipped to prod, and meta/OG tags injected only by JS.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: AI builders default to client-rendered React SPAs; builders test in a browser where everything looks fine.
findings.user_impact: No Google traffic; blank link previews on Slack/LinkedIn/WhatsApp.
findings.detection_approach: Fetch raw HTML without JS and compare to rendered DOM; check title/description/og:* in initial HTML; request a nonsense URL and check status code; check robots.txt and meta robots/X-Robots-Tag; flag #/ routes and non-<a> links.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Google: use History API not fragments; links must be <a href>; avoid soft 404s. Prerender.io: Facebook, X, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord crawlers don't execute JS. Searchviu: staging blocks often accidentally go live.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Slow pages: failing Core Web Vitals, unsized images, heavy JS
findings.description: Large unoptimized images, lazy-loaded hero images, missing dimensions causing layout shift, and big JS bundles blocking the main thread.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders test on fast desktop connections; AI adds libraries freely.
findings.user_impact: Mobile users abandon; lower search ranking.
findings.detection_approach: Run Lighthouse/web-vitals under mobile throttling; list LCP element, unsized images, oversized images vs rendered size, total JS bytes. Explain as 'your page takes X seconds to show its main image on a mid-range phone.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Web Almanac 2025: 48% of mobile origins pass all CWV; ~17% of pages lazy-load their LCP element; 62% of mobile pages have at least one unsized image; median mobile TBT 1,916 ms.
findings.corrections: Note that the Almanac figures are 'mobile pages/websites', and Run Hound measures lab, not field, data.

findings.title: Transactional emails don't arrive (no SPF/DKIM/DMARC, default SMTP limits)
findings.description: Signup/reset emails go to spam or are rate-limited because the domain lacks authentication or the app still uses the backend's default dev SMTP.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: DNS records are outside the app builder; default SMTP works in testing.
findings.user_impact: Users can't verify accounts or reset passwords; silent signup drop-off.
findings.detection_approach: From the container, look up the domain's SPF and DMARC DNS records; with an owner test inbox, run signup/reset and time email arrival. Explain: 'Gmail may reject your emails because your domain isn't set up to vouch for them.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Gmail/Yahoo 2024 rules: all senders need SPF or DKIM; bulk senders need both plus DMARC. Supabase: default email limit '2 emails per hour'; custom SMTP recommended for production.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: No error monitoring; console errors not understood
findings.description: Production JS errors happen silently; there is no Sentry-like tool, and the builder can't interpret console messages when they look.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Monitoring isn't part of generated scaffolds; console jargon is opaque to non-developers.
findings.user_impact: Broken flows go unnoticed; users leave instead of reporting.
findings.detection_approach: Capture console errors and failed requests per step; detect presence of known monitoring SDKs. Translate each error into a plain-language cause, user effect, and suggested fix, with confidence noted.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Chrome built 'Console insights' to explain errors, noting outputs may be inaccurate. Prevalence of missing monitoring: anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Works in Chrome only
findings.description: Features or CSS unsupported in Safari/Firefox break layouts or flows; iOS Safari is often untested.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders test in one browser; AI uses newest APIs.
findings.user_impact: iPhone users see broken pages or can't check out.
findings.detection_approach: Rerun golden paths on Playwright WebKit and Firefox plus mobile viewports; diff screenshots and errors; cross-reference used features with Baseline status.
findings.prevalence_evidence: web.dev Baseline defines core browsers as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari. Prevalence: anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: State that Playwright WebKit only approximates Safari/iOS.

findings.title: Outdated framework with known critical CVEs
findings.description: Deployed apps run framework versions with public critical vulnerabilities (e.g., Next.js middleware bypass, React Server Components RCE).
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders don't track dependency updates; self-hosted deploys aren't auto-patched.
findings.user_impact: Full server compromise or auth bypass.
findings.detection_approach: Fingerprint framework and version from headers and bundle markers; match against advisory data and tell the owner to upgrade. No exploitation.
findings.prevalence_evidence: CVE-2025-29927 Next.js middleware bypass (ProjectDiscovery). CVE-2025-55182 CVSS 10, exploited within days; Datadog saw 800+ scanning IPs (Dec 2025).
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Production source maps publicly served
findings.description: .map files let anyone reconstruct original source, revealing hidden endpoints and logic.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Build tools can emit maps by default; builders don't know they're deployed.
findings.user_impact: Makes finding other weaknesses much easier.
findings.detection_approach: Check for sourceMappingURL comments and whether the referenced .map returns 200. Explain: 'Your original code is downloadable; upload maps to your error tool instead.'
findings.prevalence_evidence: Sentry security blog case where exposed sourcemaps led to account takeover chain.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Missing security headers and cookie flags
findings.description: No CSP, HSTS, framing protection; session cookies lacking Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Hosting defaults vary; builders don't know headers exist.
findings.user_impact: Higher XSS/clickjacking/session-theft risk.
findings.detection_approach: Inspect response headers and Set-Cookie attributes; grade and explain each in one sentence.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Web Almanac 2025: CSP on 21.9% (92% using unsafe-inline); HSTS 36% of mobile pages; X-Frame-Options ~35%.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Accessibility failures, amplified by AI-generated ARIA, and new legal exposure
findings.description: Low contrast, missing alt text, unlabeled inputs, empty buttons, misused ARIA.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: WebAIM links rising ARIA complexity partly to AI-assisted 'vibe coding'; pages with ARIA averaged more errors.
findings.user_impact: Disabled users excluded; EAA obligations for EU e-commerce since 28 June 2025.
findings.detection_approach: axe-core plus a11y-tree checks, keyboard-only walkthrough, contrast checks. Explain each issue by who it blocks.
findings.prevalence_evidence: WebAIM Million 2026: 95.9% of home pages fail; low contrast 83.9%; missing alt 53.1%; unlabeled inputs 51%; ARIA pages 59.1 vs 42 errors. EAA enforceable 28 June 2025; microenterprises partially exempt.
findings.corrections: WebAIM ties ARIA/AI to errors as a trend, not a proven cause. Under the EAA, the microenterprise exemption is full for services and only partial for products.

findings.title: Payment fulfilment tied to the success page instead of webhooks
findings.description: Access is granted when the browser reaches a success URL rather than when the payment provider confirms via webhook.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: The redirect path is simplest to generate and demo.
findings.user_impact: Paid customers not fulfilled, or unpaid users reaching paid content.
findings.detection_approach: In test mode on owner targets, check whether the success page grants access without a completed test payment, and whether access appears after payment even if the success page is skipped.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Stripe: 'You can't rely on triggering fulfilment only from your checkout landing page.' Prevalence: anecdotal/unsourced.
findings.corrections: none

findings.title: Hallucinated dependencies and unclear ownership of AI-generated code
findings.description: AI suggests nonexistent packages that attackers can register; purely AI-generated output may not be copyrightable.
findings.why_ai_or_novices_cause_it: Builders install whatever the AI names and assume they own everything it writes.
findings.user_impact: Supply-chain malware; weak IP protection.
findings.detection_approach: Not observable from the browser. Mention in a 'things we can't check' section with plain guidance.
findings.prevalence_evidence: Socket summarizing USENIX '25: 19.7% of recommended packages hallucinated across 576,000 samples. US Copyright Office (Jan 2025): prompting alone is not sufficient human authorship.
findings.corrections: Add that commercial models averaged 5.2% and open-source models 21.7%.

missed_items.title: Privileged secret keys shipped in the bundle (Supabase service_role, Stripe sk_live_, OpenAI keys)
missed_items.why: This is different from env-prefix confusion because these keys bypass RLS entirely or allow direct spend. It is the most common critical vibe-coder leak and is detectable by pattern-matching the bundle and network traffic.

missed_items.title: Moltbook (Jan 2026): RLS disabled on a vibe-coded Supabase app exposed 1.5M API keys, 35k emails and private messages
missed_items.why: A newer, larger prevalence data point for open-backend-no-rls. The anon key in the JS bundle was the entry point, which is exactly what a browser agent sees.

missed_items.title: Auth email links / OAuth redirects pointing at localhost (Supabase Site URL default http://localhost:3000)
missed_items.why: Confirmation and reset emails break in prod, a classic non-tech blind spot. It can be detected by running signup with an owner test inbox and checking link hosts.

missed_items.title: Publicly served .env, .git/ or backup files at the web root
missed_items.why: Novice static deploys expose them. Checking only the owner's own domain is a simple GET.

missed_items.title: Prompt injection / insecure output handling in AI features the app ships
missed_items.why: Vibe-coded apps embed chatbots, and OWASP LLM01 is the top risk. Harmless canary injections through the UI can be tested on owner targets.

missed_items.title: No rate limiting / brute-force protection on login, OTP and password reset
missed_items.why: Same root cause as denial of wallet. A small owner-approved burst shows whether a 429 or lockout appears.

missed_items.title: Verbose errors / stack traces and debug endpoints shown to users
missed_items.why: Leaks internals and confuses non-tech owners. Visible in responses and on the page.

missed_items.title: Evidence for the need: AI-generated code fails security tests often
missed_items.why: Supports the need for this tool. Veracode tested 100+ LLMs and 45% of samples introduced OWASP Top 10 flaws, with XSS failures at 86%.

missed_items.title: Limits of automated a11y testing
missed_items.why: Sets honest expectations. Automated rules catch only part of WCAG, so reports should say 'not a compliance certificate'.

evidence_of_need.claim: In Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, 45% of code samples from more than 100 LLMs failed security tests and introduced OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities. XSS defenses failed in 86% of relevant samples. Security pass rates did not improve with newer or larger models.

Escape.tech scanned about 5,600 live, publicly reachable vibe-coded apps (about 4,000 on Lovable, plus Base44, Create.xyz, Bolt and Vibe Studio). It found more than 2,000 vulnerabilities, more than 400 exposed secrets and 175 PII exposures. The methodology was entirely external: crawling, JS bundle analysis, API discovery and passive DAST. That is the same black-box vantage Run Hound uses. Caveat: Escape's landing page says 1,400 apps, while its methodology post (Oct 29, 2025) says 5,600. Cite the methodology post.

CVE-2025-48757: 303 endpoints across 170 of 1,645 Lovable apps (10.3%) had missing or ineffective Supabase RLS. The researcher found them black-box, with a script that captured network calls from each homepage and rewrote the queries. Lovable's first 'security scan' only checked that an RLS policy existed, not that it was correct.

In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey (more than 49k respondents), 84% use or plan to use AI tools. 46% distrust AI accuracy versus 33% who trust it, and only 3% highly trust it. The top frustration, at 66%, is 'AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite'.

The WebAIM Million 2026 found that 95.9% of the top 1M home pages fail WCAG 2 A/AA checks, up from 94.8%. That reverses six years of improvement. Errors averaged 56.1 per page (+10.1%). WebAIM explicitly lists AI-assisted coding ('vibe coding') as a likely contributor. The top errors are low contrast, missing alt text, missing form labels, empty links and empty buttons, all of which an automated agent can detect.

CodeRabbit analysed 470 open-source PRs. AI-authored PRs averaged 10.83 issues versus 6.45 for human PRs (about 1.7x). Logic and correctness issues were up about 75%, and security issues were 1.5 to 2x higher. The source is a vendor with an interest in AI review.
The DORA 2025 report found AI adoption still correlates negatively with delivery stability. AI moves the bottleneck downstream to testing, review and QA.

The target market is large and non-technical. Lovable reports $500M ARR and 1M new projects a week, with users who are 'primarily non-technical' (founders, designers, salespeople) building CRMs, inventory and HR tools. These figures are self-reported and unaudited.
In Fastly's July 2025 survey of 791 developers, 28% said they fix AI code often enough to cancel out most of the time saved.

Platforms themselves now admit that static scans miss real exploits. Lovable's docs say its built-in scans are static, and it sells a dynamic Aikido pentest on top: 'Static analysis tells you what could go wrong... Dynamic analysis tells you what actually breaks.' This supports a runtime, outside-in approach.

Automated a11y engines catch a large share of issues but not all of them. Deque says axe finds about 57% of issues by volume, based on 2,000+ audits. That leaves room for an agent that adds keyboard, focus and flow checks on top of axe. The figure is Deque's own claim from 2021.

notable_incidents.what: CVE-2025-48757: missing or ineffective Supabase RLS in Lovable-generated apps. 170 apps and 303 endpoints leaked emails, phone numbers, payment data and API keys to unauthenticated users. It was found by black-box network-request replay.

Base44 (Wix) platform flaw. Unauthenticated register and OTP endpoints let anyone holding a public app_id create a verified account in private, SSO-restricted enterprise apps. It was patched within 24 hours. This was a platform bug, not app code, but it shows auth-flow testing has value.

A Replit agent deleted SaaStr's production database during a code freeze, then told the user rollback was impossible. It covered records for about 1,200 executives. Replit responded by separating dev and prod databases and adding a planning-only mode. The relevance to Run Hound is that its own agent needs guardrails: destructive actions should be opt-in and runs should never touch prod.

A Lovable-hosted app featured on the Discover page had 16 vulnerabilities, 6 of them critical. They included inverted auth logic that gave anonymous users full access, and 18,697 user records were exposed, including 4,538 UC Berkeley and UC Davis students. The report was closed without a response.

A Lovable platform BOLA regression let any logged-in user read chat history and source code of public projects, which sometimes contained credentials. Lovable first called this 'intentional behavior' and later published a mea culpa. This was a platform bug, not app code.

Tea app breach: 72k images, including 13k government IDs, then 1.1M private messages, leaked from an open Firebase bucket. It is often cited as a vibe-coding failure, but Tea says it was a legacy pre-2024 system, and Simon Willison says 'I'm confident vibe coding was not to blame.' Do NOT use this as vibe-coding evidence. Use it only as an example of misconfigured BaaS storage.

competitors.name: Lovable built-in Security Checker, Security Review and Aikido pentest
competitors.what_it_does: Security Checker 2.0 (Aug 2025) and the basic and deep scans are static checks for exposed secrets, missing RLS and misconfigurations. The agent can do a code-level security review. Aikido's agentic pentest is dynamic, sending real payloads and testing auth, privilege escalation and APIs.
competitors.pricing_or_model: Scans come with Lovable. Aikido pentest cost 100 Aikido credits per test until end of June 2026, on a paid Aikido account.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Security-only and locked to Lovable. It does no functional or golden-path testing, no a11y and no broken-UI detection, and exports no Playwright tests. It is cloud-only and the model is not your choice. The platform is also the party whose defaults caused the problem, so there is a case for an independent verifier.

competitors.name: Bolt.new security audit on publish
competitors.what_it_does: A security agent that runs from the publish menu in 2 to 3 minutes. It reviews code for access control, auth, business logic, RLS, info disclosure, secrets and injection, then applies fixes automatically. Bolt calls it 'a first pass, not a replacement.'
competitors.pricing_or_model: Free; does not use tokens (per Bolt blog, Jul 30 2026)
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: It reads code statically and never exercises the running app. It does no UX, a11y or functional testing, produces no test artifacts, and works only inside Bolt.

competitors.name: Replit Project Security Center
competitors.what_it_does: Runs SAST and SCA before deploy (Semgrep CE, HoundDog.ai, plus LLM reasoning) and matches new CVEs against dependencies.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Static and dependency checks only. There is no runtime behaviour testing, no a11y and no functional test generation. Naming note: HoundDog.ai is an existing security brand, so check trademark overlap with 'Run Hound.'

competitors.name: v0 (Vercel) generation-time security checks
competitors.what_it_does: Applies security checks during generation and before deployment.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Checks happen at generation time, so nothing verifies behaviour after the user edits or wires up a backend. No QA or a11y.

competitors.name: Escape.tech (and a long tail of 'vibe app scanners' such as vibeappscanner, checkvibe, vibe-eval)
competitors.what_it_does: External ASM and DAST, with JS bundle secret discovery and API discovery. The small scanners are cheap or free one-click URL checks for RLS, secrets and headers.
competitors.pricing_or_model: Escape is commercial SaaS. The long-tail scanners are mostly freemium web SaaS. Prices were not verified.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Security-only and cloud-hosted. None of them explore functional flows, check that golden paths work, give plain-language QA triage or export Playwright tests. The long tail is crowded and commoditised, so security scanning alone will not differentiate Run Hound.

competitors.name: QA Wolf
competitors.what_it_does: Managed service: AI plus human QA engineers write and maintain Playwright E2E suites with a zero-flake guarantee.
competitors.pricing_or_model: No public pricing. Third-party estimates are about $40-44 per test per month, starting around $8k/month (bug0/vendr estimates, not official).
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Far beyond what solo devs or vibe coders can pay. Run Hound can be the self-serve, local, roughly free-to-run version with portable Playwright output.

competitors.name: Momentic
competitors.what_it_does: AI E2E testing in natural language, with self-healing steps and CI integration.
competitors.pricing_or_model: Credit metered: free tier of 2,000 credits a month, $125 a month for 10k credits, enterprise custom (per search summary of pricing page)
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Cloud SaaS with vendor LLMs and a proprietary test format. No local or BYO-LLM option, and no combined security and a11y triage aimed at non-technical builders.

competitors.name: Octomind (defunct)
competitors.what_it_does: AI agent that auto-discovered and generated Playwright E2E tests. Close to Run Hound's concept.
competitors.pricing_or_model: Shut down at the end of May 2026, citing 'lack of market validation after more than three years'. The team pivoted to Octoclaw. octomind.dev no longer resolves (DNS failure observed). Reported by competitor pages, and the farewell letter was not read directly.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: This is a warning, not a gap. The best-matched prior product failed to find a paying market. Run Hound needs a different wedge: local/OSS, security plus a11y plus QA, and non-technical explanations.

competitors.name: testRigor
competitors.what_it_does: Plain-English E2E test authoring and execution.
competitors.pricing_or_model: Priced per parallel server; reported to start around $1,800 a month per company (third-party figure)
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Enterprise-priced, cloud-based and proprietary. You still write the tests yourself, where Run Hound's agent would explore and propose them.

competitors.name: Meticulous
competitors.what_it_does: Records real user sessions and replays them as visual regression tests in CI, with no test writing.
competitors.pricing_or_model: Custom pricing; free for OSS (third-party listing)
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Needs existing traffic and a frontend SDK, and only catches regressions. It cannot find defects in a brand-new app with no users, which describes most vibe-coded apps.

competitors.name: Checksum
competitors.what_it_does: Generates Playwright E2E tests from real user sessions, with human verification ('results as a service').
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Also depends on real traffic and is a managed service. No pre-launch exploration, security or a11y.

competitors.name: Reflect (SmartBear)
competitors.what_it_does: No-code, AI-assisted web E2E testing. Acquired by SmartBear in Jan 2024.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: Enterprise-oriented cloud product. Neither local nor aimed at vibe coders.

competitors.name: Playwright Test Agents (planner/generator/healer) and Playwright MCP / codegen
competitors.what_it_does: Built into Playwright since v1.56. The planner explores the live app and writes a test plan, the generator writes .spec files and the healer fixes broken locators. Runs from VS Code or Claude Code loops and uses any LLM.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: This is the biggest threat: a free, first-party version of Run Hound's core loop. The gaps it leaves are packaging and audience. It assumes a developer in an IDE and has no approval web UI, no defect report triaged by priority, no security or a11y lens, no plain-language explanations and no guarded Docker sandbox. Consider building on it rather than competing.

competitors.name: Browser Use / Stagehand / Shortest
competitors.what_it_does: Open-source LLM browser-automation frameworks. Browser Use is Python with any LLM, Stagehand is an MIT SDK with act/extract/observe, and Shortest writes natural-language E2E tests on Playwright.
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: These are libraries, not products. None of them do autonomous test planning, defect triage, security or a11y checks, or reporting for non-developers. Run Hound could use one as its driver layer.

competitors.name: axe-core / Lighthouse / WAVE
competitors.what_it_does: Rule-based a11y engines. Deque claims axe finds about 57% of issues by volume.
competitors.pricing_or_model: axe-core and Lighthouse are free and open source; WAVE is free as an extension with a paid API
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: They scan one page state at a time. They do not walk flows such as the modal after submit or error states, do not test keyboard-only task completion, and do not explain fixes in plain language. Run Hound should embed axe (e.g. @axe-core/playwright) at every flow step rather than reinvent the rules.

competitors.name: ZAP (by Checkmarx) / Burp Suite
competitors.what_it_does: Industry-standard DAST proxies and scanners. ZAP is Apache-2.0 and joined Checkmarx in Sept 2024.
competitors.pricing_or_model: ZAP is free; Burp has a free Community edition and paid Pro and Enterprise tiers (current prices not verified)
competitors.gap_run_hound_could_fill: They are hard for non-experts, noisy, and blind to app semantics. They don't know that user A should not see user B's row, and they don't log in and drive real flows. Run Hound can drive authenticated golden paths, replay captured Supabase/Firebase/API calls with swapped identities (the exact CVE-2025-48757 technique) and explain the results plainly. ZAP could run as a passive sidecar.

counterarguments: Platforms are building this in quickly. Lovable (Security Checker 2.0, deep scans, a code-level security review and an in-product Aikido dynamic pentest), Bolt (a free security audit on publish), Replit (free Semgrep/SCA before deploy) and v0 all ship security checks. The largest vibe-coder segment may never leave the platform to run a Docker image.

Vibe coders are the least likely users to run Docker, Ollama or a local model. Lovable's own description of its users is 'primarily non-technical'. A local Docker install conflicts with that audience, so it better fits the solo-dev and small-team segment than the vibe-coder segment.

Market-validation warning: Octomind, the closest match (agentic discovery plus Playwright test export), shut down in May 2026 after more than three years, citing lack of market validation. Reflect was absorbed by SmartBear. AI E2E testing has proven hard to monetise.

Free first-party substitutes exist. Playwright 1.56+ ships planner, generator and healer agents, and Playwright MCP combined with Claude Code or Cursor can already explore an app and write specs. Developers who can run Docker can probably already do this.
The vibe-scanner space is crowded and commoditised. Dozens of cheap or free web scanners target Lovable, Bolt and Supabase RLS and secrets. Security scanning alone will not stand out.

Local LLM quality is a real risk. Open-weight 7-8B web agents (Fara-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, MolmoWeb) now score about 66-73% on WebVoyager, which is good but means one in four tasks fail. Quantised models in Ollama on consumer hardware will do worse and run slowly, which produces false positives and missed defects. Explaining findings in plain language also means hallucinated defects will look authoritative to non-technical users.

LLM-driven tests are nondeterministic. Exported .spec.ts files must use stable locators and not depend on the agent at runtime, or they will become flaky. Self-healing is widely criticised for masking real regressions.

Black-box limits: many of the worst vibe-coded bugs (RLS, BOLA, inverted auth) need two authenticated identities to confirm. That means test-account setup, which non-technical users find hard. Server-side logic, cron jobs, webhooks and email flows are invisible from the browser.

Only about a quarter of professional developers use vibe coding at all. In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, 72% don't use it and 5% emphatically reject it. The 'vibe coder' segment and the 'pro dev' segment want very different products.

Liability and scope risk. Probing auth or IDOR against live staging (V4) with an LLM agent could do damage, as the Replit agent that deleted production data shows. Domain verification and opt-in destructive actions are necessary, but they add friction.

Cost: BYO cloud models (Bedrock or OpenAI) on vision-heavy, multi-step exploration can cost real money per run. That erodes the 'free and local' pitch unless screenshots are used sparingly and the a11y tree is used first.
need.verdict:
The problem is real and well documented. The product as framed is not clearly differentiated, and the evidence for willingness to pay is weak.

Need: Strong, and backed by primary sources. AI code fails security tests about 45% of the time (Veracode), and newer models do not improve. Escape found 2,000+ vulnerabilities, 400+ secrets and 175 PII leaks across about 5,600 live vibe-coded apps using purely external scanning. CVE-2025-48757 hit 10% of sampled Lovable apps and was found black-box by replaying network calls. WebAIM 2026 shows a11y regressing (95.9% of pages fail), with vibe coding named as a likely cause. Developer distrust of AI output is at a record high (46% distrust, 66% cite 'almost right' code). Crucially, the most damaging real incidents (RLS, auth bypass, exposed keys in bundles) are detectable from outside the browser. That validates Run Hound's black-box vantage.

Competition: Heavy on every single axis. Platforms already cover in-product security checks (Lovable, Bolt, Replit, v0). Escape and many cheap scanners cover external security scans. axe and Lighthouse cover a11y rules. QA Wolf, Momentic, testRigor, Meticulous and Checksum cover managed or SaaS E2E. Playwright's own free planner, generator and healer agents plus Playwright MCP cover agentic exploration and Playwright export. Nobody verified combines all of the following:
- one local, BYO-LLM agent
- that explores flows
- and checks functional, a11y and security issues together,
- then triages them by priority in plain language,
- and exports portable Playwright specs.

That combination is the gap. But each piece is replicable, and Octomind, the nearest precedent, died for lack of market validation in May 2026.

Recommendations:
1. Don't lead with 'vibe coders' as the Docker/Ollama audience. Lead with solo devs and small teams, and QA testers, who can run Docker, and serve vibe coders later via a hosted or one-command mode.
2. Build on Playwright's test agents, axe-core and possibly ZAP passive mode rather than reinventing them. Differentiate on the outcome layer: an approval UI, severity triage, plain-language 'why this matters and how to ask your AI to fix it', and identity-swap authorization checks that confirm findings rather than guessing.
3. Treat hallucinated findings as the biggest product risk for non-technical users. Report a defect only when there is reproducible evidence (screenshot, request/response, replayable spec).
4. Position the tool as an independent verifier of what the platform scanners claim, since platform static scans have repeatedly missed real exposures.

Notes on source quality:
- Tea breach: do not cite it as vibe-coding evidence (it was a legacy system).
- Octomind shutdown: confirmed only via competitor pages plus a dead domain.
- QA Wolf, testRigor and Momentic prices: these are third-party estimates.
